knowledge_statements.title: Convex Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Lagrangian duality, including weak duality and strong duality with dual attainment under a relative-interior Slater condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m,n,q\) be positive integers. Let \(f_0,\ldots,f_m:\mathbb{R}^n	o(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper closed convex functions, let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}^q\) be linear, and let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^q\). Define \(D= igcap_{i=0}^m\operatorname{dom}f_i\) and
\[p^*=\inf\{f_0(x):x\in D,\ f_i(x)\leq0\ 	ext{for }i=1,\ldots,m,\ Ax=b\}.\]
For \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\) and \(
u\in\mathbb{R}^q\), define
\[g(\lambda,
u)=\inf_{x\in D}\left(f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x)+\langle
u,Ax-bangleight),\qquad d^*=\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m,\,
u\in\mathbb{R}^q}g(\lambda,
u).\]
Weak duality gives \(d^*\leq p^*\). If \(p^*\in\mathbb{R}\) and there exists \( ar x\in\operatorname{ri}D\) such that \(A ar x=b\) and \(f_i( ar x)<0\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\), then \(d^*=p^*\), and there exist \(\lambda^*\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\) and \(
u^*\in\mathbb{R}^q\) satisfying \(g(\lambda^*,
u^*)=d^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonnegative inequality multiplier and equality multiplier produces a dual lower bound on the primal value. If the primal value is finite and a point in the relative interior of the common domain satisfies the equality constraints and all inequality constraints strictly, then the primal and dual values coincide and optimal dual multipliers exist.
assumptions_latex: \(m,n,q\) are positive integers; \(f_0,\ldots,f_m:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper closed convex functions; \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^q\) is linear; and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^q\).
\(p^*\in\mathbb{R}\).
There exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}D\) with \(A\bar x=b\) and \(f_i(\bar x)<0\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak duality gives \(d^*\leq p^*\); under the stated qualification, \(d^*=p^*\) and some \((\lambda^*,\nu^*)\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\times\mathbb{R}^q\) attains the dual supremum.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual construction architecture for a convex minimization problem
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\) be the primal space and let the primal value be \(p^\star=\inf_{x\in X}\Phi(x)\), where \(\Phi:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper and convex. A construction may additionally use a finite-dimensional perturbation space \(U\), a multiplier space \(U^*\), a cone \(K\), or an explicit constraint representation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex minimization. The definition organizes the standard Lagrangian, perturbation-conjugate, geometric, and conic routes; it does not assert strong duality or attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A dual construction architecture is a rule that augments the primal data by a family of lower bounds \(d:Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) satisfying \(d(y)\le p^\star\) for every dual-feasible \(y\in Y_{\mathrm f}\), and defines the associated dual problem as \(\sup_{y\in Y_{\mathrm f}}d(y)\). Canonical realizations are: (i) the multiplier construction \(d(\lambda,\nu)=\inf_x L(x,\lambda,\nu)\); (ii) the perturbation-conjugate construction, for \(p(u)=\inf_xF(u,x)\), given by \(d(u^*)=\inf_u\{p(u)+\langle u^*,u\rangle\}=-p^*(-u^*)\); (iii) separation of a convex epigraph or attainable set by supporting affine functionals; and (iv) conic polarity, in which multipliers belong to the dual cone \(K^*\). The output of the architecture is the pair \((Y_{\mathrm f},d)\), and its dual value is \(d^\star=\sup_{y\in Y_{\mathrm f}}d(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual construction architecture assigns to a convex primal problem a dual-feasible parameter set and a parameterized family of lower bounds on the primal value. Maximizing those bounds defines the dual problem. Standard architectures obtain the bounds from a Lagrangian, from the conjugate of a perturbation value function, from separating affine functionals, or from polar/dual cones. The definition itself guarantees only that every dual-feasible parameter gives a lower bound; equality with the primal value and attainment require separate hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A(\Phi)=(Y_{\mathrm f},d),\qquad d(y)\le p^\star\ \forall y\in Y_{\mathrm f},\qquad d^\star:=\sup_{y\in Y_{\mathrm f}}d(y)\le p^\star.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a perturbation function \(p\), the multiplier and conjugate descriptions agree whenever \(d(u^*)=\inf_u\{p(u)+\langle u^*,u\rangle\}=-p^*(-u^*)\).
A geometric construction records the same lower bound as an affine minorant \(u\mapsto d(y)-\langle y,u\rangle\) of the perturbation value function.
special_cases_latex: For \(f_i(x)\le0\) and \(h(x)=0\), take \(Y_{\mathrm f}=\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^p\) and \(d=g\), the Lagrange dual function.
For a cone constraint \(G(x)\in-K\), take its multiplier in \(K^*=\{y:\langle y,k\rangle\ge0\ \forall k\in K\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every architecture satisfying the lower-bound condition obeys weak duality \(d^\star\le p^\star\).
Different parameterizations can describe the same architecture when they induce the same feasible lower-bound family.
boundary_notes: The listed routes are construction templates, not mutually exclusive classes; a conic dual is also a Lagrangian and perturbational dual.
No constraint qualification, zero duality gap, or existence of an optimal multiplier is included in this definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lagrangian duality for inequality and equality constrained problems
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and consider \(p^\star=\inf\{f_0(x):x\in D,\ f_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ h_j(x)=0\ (j=1,\ldots,p)\}\), where the displayed functions are real-valued on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional minimization, with no convexity required for the construction. Convexity and constraint qualifications enter only in later strong-duality results.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Lagrangian is \(L:D	imes\mathbb R^m	imes\mathbb R^p	o\mathbb R\), \(L(x,\lambda,
u)=f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x)+\sum_{j=1}^p
u_jh_j(x)\). Its dual function is \(g(\lambda,
u)=\inf_{x\in D}L(x,\lambda,
u)\in\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\). Lagrangian duality associates with the primal problem the maximization \(d^\star=\sup\{g(\lambda,
u):\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m,\ 
u\in\mathbb R^p\}\). The inequality multipliers are nonnegative and the equality multipliers are unrestricted. For every primal-feasible \(x\) and every \(\lambda\ge0\), \(L(x,\lambda,
u)\le f_0(x)\), so each dual-feasible multiplier gives the lower bound \(g(\lambda,
u)\le p^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lagrangian duality adds each inequality constraint to the objective with a nonnegative multiplier and each equality constraint with an unrestricted multiplier. Minimizing this Lagrangian over the primal domain gives the dual function. Maximizing the dual function over admissible multipliers gives the Lagrange dual problem. This construction applies even to a nonconvex primal problem and always yields lower bounds for a minimization problem, although equality of primal and dual values is not part of the definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(L(x,\lambda,
u)=f_0(x)+\lambda^Tf(x)+
u^Th(x),\quad g(\lambda,
u)=\inf_{x\in D}L(x,\lambda,
u),\quad d^\star=\sup_{\lambda\ge0,
u}g(\lambda,
u)\le p^\star.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: The dual objective is the best lower bound obtained from the affine penalty family \(x\mapsto f_0(x)+\lambda^Tf(x)+\nu^Th(x)\).
Using the extended-value convention, the multiplier sign restriction can be incorporated through \(g(\lambda,\nu)=-\infty\) for \(\lambda\notin\mathbb R_+^m\).
special_cases_latex: With no equality constraints, \(g(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in D}\{f_0(x)+\lambda^Tf(x)\}\) for \(\lambda\ge0\).
With equality constraints only, every multiplier \(\nu\in\mathbb R^p\) is admissible.
immediate_consequences_latex: The function \(g\) is concave because it is a pointwise infimum of affine functions of \((\lambda,\nu)\).
Weak duality \(d^\star\le p^\star\) holds independently of primal convexity.
boundary_notes: The infimum defining \(g\) need not be attained and may equal \(-\infty\).
Strong duality and existence of optimal multipliers require additional assumptions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constraint-indicator and multiplier representations of a primal objective
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(f=(f_1,\ldots,f_m):D\to\mathbb R^m\), and let \(h:D\to\mathbb R^p\). Write \(\delta_C(z)=0\) for \(z\in C\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary finite-dimensional inequality and equality constraints. The representation is pointwise in the primal variable and uses extended-real indicators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The constrained primal objective has the hard-constraint representation \(\Phi(x)=f_0(x)+\delta_{\mathbb R_-^m}(f(x))+\delta_{\{0\}}(h(x))\) for \(x\in D\). Its Lagrangian representation is the affine multiplier family \(L(x,\lambda,
u)=f_0(x)+\lambda^Tf(x)+
u^Th(x)\), indexed by \((\lambda,
u)\in\mathbb R_+^m	imes\mathbb R^p\). These representations satisfy the pointwise identity \(\Phi(x)=\sup_{\lambda\ge0,
u\in\mathbb R^p}L(x,\lambda,
u)\): at a feasible \(x\), the supremum equals \(f_0(x)\), while violation of any displayed constraint makes it \(+\infty\). The associated lower-envelope representation in multiplier space is \(g(\lambda,
u)=\inf_{x\in D}L(x,\lambda,
u)\). Thus the same constrained model is represented by a supremum of affine multiplier penalties in primal space and by an infimum of affine functions in dual space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constrained objective can be represented either by adding extended-valued indicator functions of its constraint sets or by a family of ordinary Lagrangians indexed by admissible multipliers. Pointwise maximization of the Lagrangian over all admissible multipliers recovers the hard constrained objective exactly. Pointwise minimization over the primal variable instead produces the dual function. These are two different envelopes of the same Lagrangian family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\Phi(x)=f_0(x)+\delta_{\mathbb R_-^m}(f(x))+\delta_{\{0\}}(h(x))=\sup_{\lambda\ge0,
u}L(x,\lambda,
u),\qquad g(\lambda,
u)=\inf_{x\in D}L(x,\lambda,
u).\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: Each scalar indicator obeys \(\delta_{(-\infty,0]}(t)=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}\lambda t\), and \(\delta_{\{0\}}(s)=\sup_{\nu\in\mathbb R}\nu s\).

The primal value is \(\inf_{x\in D}\sup_{\lambda\ge0,
u}L(x,\lambda,
u)\), whereas the dual value is \(\sup_{\lambda\ge0,
u}\inf_{x\in D}L(x,\lambda,
u)\).
special_cases_latex: A set constraint \(x\in C\) is represented by adding \(\delta_C(x)\) to the objective.
For affine equalities \(Ax=b\), the equality term is \(\nu^T(Ax-b)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The primal and dual constructions differ only in the order of \(\inf_x\) and \(\sup_{\lambda,\nu}\).
The minimax inequality immediately gives the value relation \(d^\star\le p^\star\).
boundary_notes: The pointwise supremum identity does not imply that a finite maximizing multiplier exists at an infeasible point.
Interchanging the infimum and supremum requires a separate minimax or strong-duality condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Concavity of the Ordinary Dual Function
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ordinary dual function is concave in the multipliers because it is a pointwise infimum of affine functions; primal convexity is unnecessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(L(x,\lambda,
u)=f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x)+\langle
u,h(x)angle\), the function \(g(\lambda,
u)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda,
u)\) is concave in \((\lambda,
u)\) on \(\mathbb R^m	imes\mathbb R^p\), even when the primal functions are not convex.
assumptions_latex: \(X\ne\varnothing\), and \(L(x,\lambda,\nu)\) is defined for the displayed multipliers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is concave on \(\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^p\), hence also on \(\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^p\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural property of the dual function generated by finitely many ordinary constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Multiplier-Supremum Feasibility Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximizing over sign-compatible ordinary multipliers leaves the objective unchanged at feasible points and gives positive infinity at infeasible points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in X\),
\[
\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m,\,\nu\in\mathbb R^p}L(x,\lambda,\nu)=
\begin{cases}
f_0(x),&f_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ h(x)=0,\\
+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Consequently, the constrained primal value equals \(\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{\lambda\ge0,\nu}L(x,\lambda,\nu)\).
assumptions_latex: \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to\mathbb R\) and \(h:X\to\mathbb R^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf\{f_0(x):f_i(x)\le0,\ h(x)=0\}=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{\lambda\ge0,\nu}L(x,\lambda,\nu)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise feasibility representation specific to ordinary scalar inequalities and equalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary Constraint Lagrangians
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scalar inequality and affine equality constraints enter the Lagrangian through nonnegative and unrestricted multipliers, respectively. Minimization over the primal variable produces a lower bound on every feasible objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the problem \(\inf\{f_0(x):x\in X,\ f_i(x)\leq0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ h(x)=0\}\), the ordinary constraint Lagrangian is
\[
L(x,\lambda,
u)=f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x)+\langle
u,h(x)angle,
\]
where \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\) and \(
u\in\mathbb R^p\). Its dual function is \(g(\lambda,
u)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda,
u)\). Every primal-feasible \(x\) satisfies \(g(\lambda,
u)\leq L(x,\lambda,
u)\leq f_0(x)\).
assumptions_latex: \(m,p\in\mathbb N\), \(X\neq\varnothing\) is a subset of a real vector space, \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to\mathbb R\), and \(h:X\to\mathbb R^p\) is affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(\lambda,\nu)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda,\nu)\) is the associated dual function and is a lower bound on every primal-feasible objective value.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite families of scalar inequalities and affine equality constraints.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concavity and Upper Semicontinuity of the Ordinary Dual Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier-space structure of the dual function generated by an ordinary finite scalar-constraint Lagrangian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Extend \(g(\lambda,
u)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda,
u)\) to \(\mathbb R^m	imes\mathbb R^p\). Then \(g\) is concave and upper semicontinuous, possibly taking the value \(-\infty\). Consequently every superlevel set \(\{(\lambda,
u):g(\lambda,
u)\geq\alpha\}\) is closed and convex. These conclusions do not require convexity of the primal functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ordinary dual function is concave and upper semicontinuous in the multipliers because it is the pointwise infimum of continuous affine functions, even for a nonconvex primal problem.
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\varnothing\).
\(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to\mathbb R\) and \(h:X\to\mathbb R^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is concave and upper semicontinuous, and its superlevel sets are closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Concavity and Upper Semicontinuity of the Ordinary Dual Function

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Multiplier Supremum Representation of Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise representation supplied specifically by ordinary scalar and equality multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in X\),
\[
\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m,\,\nu\in\mathbb R^p}L(x,\lambda,\nu)=
\begin{cases}
f_0(x),&f_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ h(x)=0,\\
+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Consequently the constrained primal value equals \(\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{\lambda\ge0,\nu}L(x,\lambda,\nu)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximizing the ordinary Lagrangian over sign-compatible multipliers leaves the objective unchanged at feasible points and diverges at infeasible points.
assumptions_latex: \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to\mathbb R\) and \(h:X\to\mathbb R^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf\{f_0(x):f_i(x)\le0,\ h(x)=0\}=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{\lambda\ge0,\nu}L(x,\lambda,\nu).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Multiplier Supremum Representation of Feasibility
Convexity of Cone-Inequality Lagrangian Slices
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive-dual-cone scalarization converts a cone-convex constraint map into a convex scalar function, making each admissible-multiplier Lagrangian slice convex in the primal variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be convex, let \(f_0:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex, and let \(G:X\to Y\) be \(K\)-convex in the sense that
\[
G(tx+(1-t)z)\preceq_K tG(x)+(1-t)G(z)
\]
for \(t\in[0,1]\). Then for every \(y\in K^*\), the scalarization \(x\mapsto\langle y,G(x)\rangle\) is convex, and consequently
\[
L(x,y)=f_0(x)+\langle y,G(x)\rangle
\]
is convex in \(x\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
\(X\) is convex, \(f_0\) is convex, \(G\) is \(K\)-convex, and \(y\in K^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The functions \(x\mapsto\langle y,G(x)\rangle\) and \(x\mapsto L(x,y)\) are convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-variable convexity induced by cone convexity and positive-dual-cone scalarization.

knowledge_statements.title: Orthant Specialization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ordinary nonnegative-multiplier Lagrangian is precisely the generalized cone Lagrangian for the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(Y=\mathbb R^m\) and \(K=\mathbb R_+^m\), one has \(K^*=K\). Writing \(G(x)=(f_1(x),\ldots,f_m(x))\), the cone constraint \(G(x)\preceq_K0\) is exactly \(f_i(x)\leq0\) for every \(i\), and
\[
L(x,\lambda)=f_0(x)+\langle\lambda,G(x)\rangle=f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x),\qquad \lambda\geq0.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(Y=\mathbb R^m\) with its standard inner product.
\(K=\mathbb R_+^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generalized inequality and Lagrangian reduce exactly to componentwise inequalities and nonnegative scalar multipliers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reduction of the cone Lagrangian to finitely many scalar inequality multipliers.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Inequality Lagrangians
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone inequality is paired with a multiplier from the dual cone; the resulting Lagrangian infimum gives a lower bound on every feasible objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Write \(G(x)\preceq_K0\) when \(-G(x)\in K\), and define \(K^*=\{y\in Y:\langle y,k\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }k\in K\}\). For
\[
\inf\{f_0(x):x\in X,\ G(x)\preceq_K0\},
\]
the generalized-inequality Lagrangian is \(L(x,y)=f_0(x)+\langle y,G(x)\rangle\), with \(y\in K^*\), and \(g(y)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)\). If \(x\) is feasible, then \(\langle y,G(x)\rangle\leq0\), hence \(g(y)\leq f_0(x)\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space \(Y\).
\(G:X\to Y\) and \(f_0:X\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(y\in K^*\), \(g(y)=\inf_{x\in X}[f_0(x)+\langle y,G(x)\rangle]\) is a primal lower bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cone-ordered inequalities in finite-dimensional inner-product spaces.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Admissible Cone of Generalized-Inequality Multipliers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp characterization of multipliers preserving the weak-duality sign for every cone-feasible residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq Y\) be a closed convex cone and use \(G(x)\preceq_K0\iff G(x)\in-K\). Then
\[
y\in K^*\iff \langle y,v\rangle\leq0\quad\text{for every }v\in-K.
\]
Thus \(K^*\) is exactly the multiplier set for which \(f_0(x)+\langle y,G(x)\rangle\leq f_0(x)\) holds for every cone-feasible residual. If \(y\notin K^*\), some \(k\in K\) satisfies \(\langle y,k\rangle<0\), and the feasible residual \(-k\) has \(\langle y,-k\rangle>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive dual cone is exactly the set of multipliers whose pairing has the required sign on every feasible cone residual.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
Feasible residuals lie in \(-K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\in K^*\iff \langle y,v\rangle\leq0\ \forall v\in-K\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Admissible Cone of Generalized-Inequality Multipliers

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ordinary Inequalities as an Orthant Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reduction of the cone Lagrangian to finitely many scalar inequality multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(Y=\mathbb R^m\) and \(K=\mathbb R_+^m\), one has \(K^*=K\). Writing \(G(x)=(f_1(x),\ldots,f_m(x))\), the cone constraint \(G(x)\preceq_K0\) is exactly \(f_i(x)\le0\) for all \(i\), and
\[
L(x,\lambda)=f_0(x)+\langle\lambda,G(x)\rangle=f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x),\qquad \lambda\ge0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ordinary nonnegative-multiplier Lagrangian is precisely the generalized cone Lagrangian for the nonnegative orthant.

\(K=\mathbb R_+^m\).

knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary Inequalities as an Orthant Specialization
Closure Produced by Double Partial Conjugation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonclosed convex perturbation slice, double partial conjugation recovers its lower-semicontinuous closure rather than necessarily the original slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(F(x,\cdot)\) is proper convex but not lower semicontinuous, then reconstruction from \(L(x,y^*)=-F(x,\cdot)^*(y^*)\) yields
\[
\sup_{y^*}\bigl(\langle y^*,u\rangle+L(x,y^*)\bigr)=F(x,\cdot)^{**}(u)=\operatorname{cl}F(x,\cdot)(u),
\]
which may be strictly smaller than \(F(x,u)\).
assumptions_latex: For the fixed \(x\), \(F(x,\cdot)\) is proper and convex but need not be lower semicontinuous.
\(U\) is finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{y^*}[\langle y^*,u\rangle+L(x,y^*)]=F(x,\cdot)^{**}(u)\leq F(x,u)\), with possible strict inequality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for exact reconstruction of a nonclosed perturbation slice.

notation.meaning: biconjugate or lower-semicontinuous convex closure of the slice

knowledge_statements.title: Reconstruction from the Extended-Valued Lagrangian
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed convex perturbation slice is reconstructed exactly as the supremum of its affine Lagrangian representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose that for a fixed \(x\), the slice \(F(x,\cdot)\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and define
\[
L(x,y^*)=-F(x,\cdot)^*(y^*).
\]
Then Fenchel-Moreau biconjugacy gives
\[
F(x,u)=\sup_{y^*\in U^*}\bigl(\langle y^*,u\rangle+L(x,y^*)\bigr).
\]
Thus partial conjugation is lossless on proper closed convex slices.
assumptions_latex: For the fixed \(x\), \(F(x,\cdot)\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(U\) is finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x,u)=\sup_{y^*}[\langle y^*,u\rangle+L(x,y^*)]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Biconjugate recovery of each closed convex perturbation slice from its Lagrangian.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Valued Lagrangian Models
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-valued perturbation function yields a Lagrangian by partial conjugation; indicator values can encode hard constraints, and the dual function is a slice of the negative full conjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(x\in X\) and \(y^*\in U^*\), define the extended-valued Lagrangian by
\[
L(x,y^*)=\inf_{u\in U}\bigl(F(x,u)-\langle y^*,u\rangle\bigr)=-F(x,\cdot)^*(y^*).
\]
The associated dual function satisfies
\[
g(y^*)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y^*)=-\sup_{(x,u)\in X\times U}\bigl(\langle y^*,u\rangle-F(x,u)\bigr)=-F^*(0,y^*).
\]
Indicator functions embedded in \(F\) can encode hard constraints without a separate restriction of the infimum domain.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(U\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces, with dual space \(U^*\).
\(F:X\times U\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper and convex, and the unperturbed primal value is \(\inf_{x\in X}F(x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbation representation incorporating constraints through infinite values.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

u)=f_0(x)+\sum_i\lambda_if_i(x)+\sum_j

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-valued Lagrangian incorporates an implicit primal-domain constraint by assigning infinite cost outside that domain. Minimizing it over the whole ambient space is exactly the same as minimizing the ordinary Lagrangian over the retained domain. For convex data and nonnegative inequality multipliers, the extended-valued Lagrangian remains convex in the primal variable.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Family of Lagrange dual lower bounds
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For a primal minimization problem with nonempty domain \(D\), let \(L(x,y)\) be a Lagrangian, where \(y\) denotes all inequality and equality multipliers and \(Y_{\mathrm f}\) is the multiplier sign cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The family is defined for arbitrary primal data; convexity of the primal functions is unnecessary for concavity of the dual function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The dual-function family is the collection of primal infima \(\{g(y):y\in Y_{\mathrm f}\}\) generated by \(g(y)=\inf_{x\in D}L(x,y)\). Equivalently, each \(y\) selects the lower-bounding function \(x\mapsto L(x,y)\), and \(g(y)\) is its greatest constant lower bound. For ordinary constraints, \(y=(\lambda,
u)\), \(Y_{\mathrm f}=\mathbb R_+^m	imes\mathbb R^p\), and \(g(\lambda,
u)=\inf_{x\in D}\{f_0(x)+\lambda^Tf(x)+
u^Th(x)\}\). The effective members are those with \(g(y)>-\infty\). The pointwise infimum construction makes \(g\) concave on its multiplier space, and every effective feasible member satisfies \(g(y)\le p^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual-function family consists of all lower bounds obtained by fixing admissible multipliers and minimizing the corresponding Lagrangian over the primal domain. Some members may be the vacuous value minus infinity. The effective members are finite lower bounds. As a function of the multipliers, the family forms a concave dual function even if the primal problem is not convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(y):=\inf_{x\in D}L(x,y),\qquad \mathcal G:=\{g(y):y\in Y_{\mathrm f}\},\qquad g(y)\le p^\star\ \forall y\in Y_{\mathrm f}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(g(y)=\sup\{\alpha\in\mathbb R:L(x,y)\ge\alpha\ \forall x\in D\}\), with value \(-\infty\) when no finite constant lower bound exists.
The hypograph of g is \(\{(y,\alpha):\alpha\le L(x,y)\ \forall x\in D\}\).
special_cases_latex: When D is finite, \(g\) is the pointwise minimum of finitely many affine functions of y.
When L is strictly convex and coercive in x for fixed y, the family member is attained at a unique primal minimizer.
immediate_consequences_latex: Maximizing over the family selects the best Lagrangian lower bound.
The effective dual domain is convex because it is the effective domain of the convex function \(-g\).
boundary_notes: The family may contain only vacuous lower bounds in degenerate problems.
Attainment of the inner infimum is not part of the definition.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Slice Polyhedral Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum of finitely many affine Lagrangian slices is a concave polyhedral dual function that is piecewise affine on its active-set regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If
\[
g(y)=\min_{1\le j\le N}\bigl(a_j+\langle b_j,y\rangle\bigr),
\]
then \(g\) is a concave polyhedral function and
\[
\operatorname{hypo}g=\bigcap_{j=1}^N\{(y,t):t\le a_j+\langle b_j,y\rangle\}.
\]
Consequently, its hypograph is a polyhedron and \(g\) is affine on each polyhedral region on which the active-index set is fixed.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is finite-dimensional.
\(g\) is the pointwise minimum of finitely many finite affine functions \(y\mapsto a_j+\langle b_j,y\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is a concave polyhedral function, its hypograph is a polyhedron, and it is affine on each region having a fixed active-index set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite affine-envelope specialization of dual-function geometry.

notation.meaning: intercept and slope of the \(j\)-th affine slice

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Function Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual function is an upper-semicontinuous concave infimum of affine Lagrangian slices, and its hypograph is the intersection of their halfspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(g(y)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)\), allowing the value \(-\infty\). Then \(g\) is concave because it is a pointwise infimum of affine functions. Moreover,
\[
\operatorname{hypo}g=\{(y,t):t\leq g(y)\}=\bigcap_{x\in X}\{(y,t):t\leq L(x,y)\}.
\]
Each set in the intersection is a closed halfspace, so \(g\) is upper semicontinuous. Equivalently, \(-g\) is a lower-semicontinuous convex extended-valued function.
assumptions_latex: For every \(x\in X\), \(L(x,\cdot)\) is finite affine on a finite-dimensional multiplier space \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\cdot)\) is concave and upper semicontinuous, with \(\operatorname{hypo}g=\bigcap_{x\in X}\operatorname{hypo}L(x,\cdot)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of an infimum of multiplier-affine Lagrangian slices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global regularity obtained when all affine Lagrangian slices have uniformly bounded slopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose
\[
L(x,y)=a(x)+\langle b(x),y\rangle,
\qquad g(y)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y),
\]
where \(X\ne\varnothing\), and \(\sup_{x\in X}\|b(x)\|_*\le M<\infty\). If \(g(y_0)>-\infty\) at some \(y_0\), then \(g\) is finite everywhere and
\[
|g(y)-g(z)|\le M\|y-z\|\qquad(y,z\in Y).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper infimum of affine slices with uniformly bounded slopes is an everywhere-finite globally Lipschitz concave function.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is finite-dimensional and normed, and \(X\ne\varnothing\).
\(L(x,y)=a(x)+\langle b(x),y\rangle\).
\(\sup_x\|b(x)\|_*\le M<\infty\).
\(g(y_0)>-\infty\) for some \(y_0\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g:Y\to\mathbb R\) and \(|g(y)-g(z)|\le M\|y-z\|\) for all \(y,z\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Slope Lipschitz Geometry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral specialization of the hypograph-intersection representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If
\[
g(y)=\min_{1\le i\le m}\{\alpha_i+\langle b_i,y\rangle\},
\]
then \(g\) is a finite-valued concave polyhedral function and
\[
\operatorname{hypo}g= igcap_{i=1}^m\{(y,t):t\le\alpha_i+\langle b_i,y\rangle\}
\]
is a polyhedron. Conversely, every finite-valued concave polyhedral function admits such a finite minimum-of-affine representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-valued concave polyhedral functions are exactly finite minima of affine functions, equivalently functions with polyhedral hypographs.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is finite-valued concave polyhedral if and only if it is a finite pointwise minimum of finite affine functions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hypograph geometry of a Lagrange dual function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(L(x,y)=a(x)+\langle b(x),y\rangle\) be affine in \(y\in\mathbb R^q\) for every \(x\in D\), and define \(g(y)=\inf_{x\in D}L(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional multiplier space. Values of g may equal minus infinity; geometric assertions concern its hypograph and upper level sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual-function geometry is the hypograph system generated by the affine majorants \(L(x,\cdot)\): \(\operatorname{hypo}g=\{(y,t)\in\mathbb R^q\times\mathbb R:t\le g(y)\}=\bigcap_{x\in D}\{(y,t):t\le a(x)+\langle b(x),y\rangle\}\). Consequently, \(\operatorname{hypo}g\) is convex and g is concave. For every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), the upper level set is \(\{y:g(y)\ge\alpha\}=\bigcap_{x\in D}\{y:a(x)+\langle b(x),y\rangle\ge\alpha\}\), an intersection of closed halfspaces when each affine member is finite. The dual optimization problem seeks the largest height t for which the hypograph intersects the admissible multiplier cylinder \(Y_{\mathrm f}\times\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Geometrically, a dual function is the lower envelope of affine functions of the multipliers. Its hypograph is the intersection of the halfspaces lying below every affine member of the Lagrangian family. This makes the hypograph convex and the dual function concave. Maximizing the dual function amounts to finding the highest point of this hypograph over the admissible multiplier set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{hypo}g=\bigcap_{x\in D}\{(y,t):t\le L(x,y)\},\qquad \{y:g(y)\ge\alpha\}=\bigcap_{x\in D}\{y:L(x,y)\ge\alpha\}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: Concavity is expressed by \(g(\theta y_1+(1-\theta)y_2)\ge\theta g(y_1)+(1-\theta)g(y_2)\) for \(0\le\theta\le1\).
The negative dual function \(-g\) is the pointwise supremum of the affine functions \(-L(x,\cdot)\) and is convex.
special_cases_latex: For finite D, g is polyhedral concave.
If the minimizing x is locally unique and varies smoothly, g can be differentiable even though the general lower envelope is nonsmooth.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every upper level set of g is convex.
Explicit equations restricting the finite domain of g appear as vertical faces or lower-dimensional affine hull constraints in its hypograph.
boundary_notes: Closedness of the hypograph follows from the displayed intersection when all affine members are finite, but g may still be improper.
Concavity alone does not imply differentiability or dual attainment.

notation.meaning: hypograph of the concave dual function
intercept and multiplier coefficient of a Lagrangian member

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Effective, feasible, and improper regimes of a dual function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let D be nonempty, let the Lagrangian be finite-valued on \(D\times Y\), and define \(g(y)=\inf_{x\in D}L(x,y)\in\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\). Let \(Y_{\mathrm sign}\subseteq Y\) impose the multiplier sign restrictions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary finite-valued Lagrangian models. In more general extended-valued models, a positive-infinity regime must be handled separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The effective dual domain is \(\operatorname{dom}g=\{y\in Y:g(y)>-\infty\}\). It partitions multiplier space into the finite regime \(Y_{\mathrm fin}=\operatorname{dom}g\), where the Lagrangian is bounded below in x and g supplies a real lower bound, and the unbounded-below regime \(Y_{-\infty}=Y\setminus\operatorname{dom}g\), where \(g(y)=-\infty\). The dual-feasible domain is \(Y_{\mathrm df}=Y_{\mathrm sign}\cap\operatorname{dom}g\). Points satisfying the sign conditions but lying in \(Y_{-\infty}\) are formally admissible for an extended-valued maximization but yield only a vacuous bound. For ordinary inequalities and equalities, \(Y_{\mathrm sign}=\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplier space separates into a finite regime, where the Lagrangian is bounded below in the primal variable, and a minus-infinity regime, where it is unbounded below. Dual feasibility combines membership in the finite regime with the sign restrictions on inequality multipliers. A sign-admissible point with dual value minus infinity contributes only a vacuous lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}g=\{y:g(y)>-\infty\},\quad Y_{-\infty}=\{y:g(y)=-\infty\},\quad Y_{\mathrm df}=Y_{\mathrm sign}\cap\operatorname{dom}g.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\in\operatorname{dom}g\) if and only if there exists \(\beta\in\mathbb R\) such that \(L(x,y)\ge\beta\) for every \(x\in D\).
\(y\in Y_{-\infty}\) if and only if for every \(M\in\mathbb R\) there exists \(x\in D\) with \(L(x,y)<M\).
special_cases_latex: For a quadratic Lagrangian, finiteness commonly imposes positive-semidefiniteness and a range condition.
For a linear program, finiteness of g commonly produces explicit affine equalities or inequalities in the dual variables.
immediate_consequences_latex: The effective domain of a concave dual function is convex.
The dual problem can be written either with g extended by minus infinity or with \(\operatorname{dom}g\) imposed explicitly.
boundary_notes: If D is empty or the Lagrangian may equal positive infinity everywhere, g can equal positive infinity; that case is excluded here.
A finite dual value does not imply that the primal infimum defining it is attained.

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate Preimage Representation of the Effective Dual Domain
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an affine-equality Lagrangian, the effective dual domain is the inverse image of the objective conjugate's domain under the negative adjoint map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, let \(A:X\to Z\) be linear, let \(b\in Z\), and for \(y\in Z^*\) set \(L(x,y)=f(x)+\langle y,Ax-b\rangle\). Then \[g(y)=\inf_xL(x,y)=-f^*(-A^*y)-\langle y,b\rangle,\] and therefore \[\operatorname{dom}g=\{y\in Z^*:-A^*y\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\}=(-A^*)^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}f^*).\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Z\) are finite-dimensional paired real vector spaces.
\(f\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(A:X\to Z\) is linear and \(b\in Z\).
\(L(x,y)=f(x)+\langle y,Ax-b\rangle\) for \(y\in Z^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(y)=-f^*(-A^*y)-\langle y,b\rangle,\qquad\operatorname{dom}g=(-A^*)^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}f^*).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact domain formula for an affine-equality Lagrangian on paired finite-dimensional spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Effective Dual Domain
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective dual domain consists of multipliers for which the Lagrangian has a finite lower bound; concavity makes this domain convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The effective dual domain is
\[
\operatorname{dom}g:=\{y\in Y:g(y)>-\infty\}.
\]
For \(g(y)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)\), membership means that the Lagrangian is bounded below over \(X\) at multiplier \(y\). Since \(g\) is concave, if \(y_0,y_1\in\operatorname{dom}g\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\), then
\[
g((1-\theta)y_0+\theta y_1)\geq(1-\theta)g(y_0)+\theta g(y_1)>-\infty,
\]
so \(\operatorname{dom}g\) is convex.
assumptions_latex: \(g:Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) is a Lagrangian dual function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}g=\{y\in Y:g(y)>-\infty\}\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective domain for a concave dual function that may equal \(-\infty\).

knowledge_statements.title: Regularity in the Everywhere-Finite Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An everywhere-finite concave dual function on a finite-dimensional multiplier space is continuous and locally Lipschitz; it is Lipschitz on compact convex subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(g:Y\to\mathbb R\) be concave. Then \(g\) is continuous and locally Lipschitz at every point of \(Y\). More precisely, \(g\) is Lipschitz on every compact convex subset of \(Y\). Thus an everywhere-finite Lagrange dual function has no effective-domain boundary discontinuity.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(g:Y\to\mathbb R\) is concave and finite everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is continuous on \(Y\), locally Lipschitz at every point, and Lipschitz on each compact convex subset of \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity forced by concavity when the effective dual domain is the entire finite-dimensional multiplier space.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Valued Dual Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual function is finite-valued everywhere exactly when every multiplier-fixed Lagrangian is bounded below; nonempty compactness and continuity provide a standard sufficient condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The dual function \(g(y)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)\) is in a finite-valued regime on \(Y\) precisely when
\[
\operatorname{dom}g=Y,
\]
equivalently, when \(L(\cdot,y)\) is bounded below on \(X\) for every \(y\in Y\). A sufficient condition is that \(X\) be compact and that \(L\) be continuous on \(X\times Y\); then each infimum is attained and belongs to \(\mathbb R\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\varnothing\) is a set, \(Y\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space, and \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) is real-valued.
\(g(y)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)\) for every \(y\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The finite-valued regime is \(\operatorname{dom}g=Y\), equivalently \(\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)>-\infty\) for every \(y\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criteria ensuring the dual function is real-valued everywhere.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A noncompact sufficient condition for an everywhere finite-valued dual function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\), and let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\). If, for every \(y\in Y\), the function \(L(\cdot,y)\) is lower semicontinuous and coercive, then it attains a finite minimum. Consequently,
\[
g(y)=\min_{x\in X}L(x,y)\in\mathbb R\qquad(y\in Y),

Affine Lagrangian Finiteness Dichotomy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine function minimized over the whole primal space is finite exactly when its linear coefficient vanishes; otherwise its infimum is minus infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional vector space and suppose \[L(x,y)=c(y)+\langle a(y),x\rangle\qquad(x\in X),\] where \(c(y)\in\mathbb R\) and \(a(y)\in X^*\). Then \[g(y)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)=\begin{cases}c(y),&a(y)=0,\\-\infty,&a(y)\ne0.\end{cases}\] Consequently \(\operatorname{dom}g=\{y:a(y)=0\}\); if \(a\) is affine, this domain is an affine set, possibly empty or lower-dimensional.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Valued Dual Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extended-valued dual behavior arises when a multiplier-fixed Lagrangian is unbounded below; the elementary bilinear Lagrangian shows that the effective domain can collapse to one point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The extended-valued regime occurs when \(g(y)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)=-\infty\) for at least one \(y\in Y\). Equivalently, there exist \(y\in Y\) and a sequence \((x_k)\subset X\) such that \(L(x_k,y)\to-\infty\). Then \(y\notin\operatorname{dom}g\), and maximizing \(g\) may be restricted without loss to \(\operatorname{dom}g\). For example, \(L(x,y)=yx\) on \(X=\mathbb R\) gives \(g(0)=0\) and \(g(y)=-\infty\) for every \(y\neq0\).
assumptions_latex: \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) is real-valued and affine in its second argument.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If some \(L(\cdot,y)\) is unbounded below, then \(g(y)=-\infty\) and \(\operatorname{dom}g\subsetneq Y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of finiteness through unbounded Lagrangian minimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Radial Continuity at Finite Dual-Domain Boundary Points
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper upper-semicontinuous concave dual function approaches each finite boundary value continuously along segments from its relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) be proper, concave, and upper semicontinuous on a finite-dimensional space. For \(y_0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\) and \(\bar y\in\operatorname{dom}g\), \[\lim_{t\uparrow1}g((1-t)y_0+t\bar y)=g(\bar y).\] Thus boundary discontinuity cannot occur along a fixed segment approaching a finite domain point from the relative interior, although unrestricted approaches can still fail to be continuous.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Domain Boundary Behavior
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper dual function is continuous on the relative interior of its effective domain, but boundary continuity can fail; upper semicontinuity still rules out excessive limiting values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A proper concave dual function \(g\) is continuous relative to \(\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}g)\) at every point of \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\). At any \(\bar y\in\operatorname{dom}g\), upper semicontinuity gives
\[
\limsup_{y\to\bar y}g(y)\leq g(\bar y).
\]
Continuity need not extend to \(\operatorname{rbd}(\operatorname{dom}g)\); thus boundary multiplier sequences may have dual values strictly below the value at their limit, although an upward jump beyond \(g(\bar y)\) is excluded.
assumptions_latex: \(g:Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) is proper, concave, and upper semicontinuous.
\(Y\) is finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is continuous on \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\), while \(\limsup_{y\to\bar y}g(y)\leq g(\bar y)\) at every boundary point \(\bar y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuity internally and upper-semicontinuous behavior at the effective-domain boundary.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary Continuity Can Fail Along Nonradial Approaches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed concave example separating upper semicontinuity and radial continuity from full relative-domain continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(g:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) by
\[
g(u,v)=\begin{cases}-v^2/u,&u>0,\\0,&(u,v)=(0,0),\\-\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
\]
Then \(g\) is proper, concave, and upper semicontinuous, with
\[
\operatorname{dom}g=\{(u,v):u>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.
\]
Although \(g(0,0)=0\), the domain sequence \((u,\sqrt u)\to(0,0)\) satisfies \(g(u,\sqrt u)=-1\). Hence \(g\) is not continuous at this effective-domain boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative quadratic perspective is closed and concave but discontinuous at the origin along a curved domain sequence.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is defined by the displayed extended-valued formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is upper semicontinuous and concave but is not continuous at \((0,0)\in\operatorname{rbd}(\operatorname{dom}g)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial Continuity at Finite Boundary Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided continuity along segments from the relative interior to a finite effective-domain boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

\[
\lim_{t\uparrow1}g((1-t)y_0+t\bar y)=g(\bar y).
\]
Thus full boundary continuity may fail, but continuity holds along every such segment.

Differentiability from Coincident Active Slopes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual function is differentiable exactly when all active Lagrangian minimizers have the same multiplier slope; a unique minimizer is sufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the seed hypotheses, \(g\) is differentiable at \(y\) if and only if all active slopes coincide: there is a \(v\in Y\) such that
\[
\nabla_yL(x,y)=v\qquad\text{for every }x\in M(y).
\]
In that case \(\nabla g(y)=v\). In particular, uniqueness of the Lagrangian minimizer is sufficient, but not necessary, for differentiability.
assumptions_latex: The hypotheses of the seed Danskin representation hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is differentiable at \(y\) if and only if \(\{\nabla_yL(x,y):x\in M(y)\}\) is a singleton; its unique element is \(\nabla g(y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact differentiability criterion within the compact Danskin regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Derivative of a Dual Function
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional derivative of the dual function is the minimum of the active multiplier slopes in the requested direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the compactness and continuity hypotheses ensuring \(M(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}L(x,y)\neq\varnothing\), the one-sided directional derivative of \(g(y)=\min_{x\in X}L(x,y)\) is
\[
g'(y;d)=\min_{x\in M(y)}\langle\nabla_yL(x,y),d\rangle.
\]
assumptions_latex: The hypotheses of the seed Danskin representation hold.
\(d\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g'(y;d)=\min_{x\in M(y)}\langle\nabla_yL(x,y),d\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional form of Danskin's theorem for a minimum of differentiable affine multiplier slices.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Function Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under compactness and the stated continuity assumptions, dual supergradients are convex combinations of constraint-residual slopes at Lagrangian minimizers; their negatives are subgradients of the convex function minus the dual function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(y\in Y\), let
\[
g(y)=\min_{x\in X}L(x,y),\qquad M(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}L(x,y).
\]
Then \(M(y)\neq\varnothing\), and the concave superdifferential satisfies
\[
\partial^+g(y)=\operatorname{conv}\{\nabla_yL(x,y):x\in M(y)\}.
\]
Equivalently, for the convex function \(-g\),
\[
\partial(-g)(y)=-\operatorname{conv}\{\nabla_yL(x,y):x\in M(y)\}.
\]
For an ordinary Lagrangian, each active slope is the vector of constraint residuals evaluated at a Lagrangian minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\varnothing\) is a compact topological space and \(Y\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) is continuous; for every \(x\in X\), \(L(x,\cdot)\) is affine and differentiable; and \(x\mapsto\nabla_yL(x,y)\) is continuous for every \(y\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(-g)(y)=-\operatorname{conv}\{\nabla_yL(x,y):x\in M(y)\}\) for every \(y\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Danskin representation for the convex subdifferential of the negative dual function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Superdifferential of a concave dual function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(q:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) be a proper concave dual function, and let \(\lambda_0\in\operatorname{dom}q\). For the inequality model, \(q(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+\lambda^Tc(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonsmooth dual geometry. The term superdifferential is used to avoid the sign ambiguity that arises when some texts call concave supporting slopes subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual-function superdifferential at \(\lambda_0\) is \(\partial^+q(\lambda_0)=\{s\in\mathbb R^m:q(\lambda)\le q(\lambda_0)+s^T(\lambda-\lambda_0)\ \forall\lambda\in\mathbb R^m\}\). Equivalently, \(s\in\partial^+q(\lambda_0)\) if and only if \(-s\in\partial(-q)(\lambda_0)\). If the infimum defining q at \(\lambda_0\) is attained at \(x_0\), then the constraint-residual vector is a supporting slope: \(c(x_0)\in\partial^+q(\lambda_0)\), or equivalently \(-c(x_0)\in\partial(-q)(\lambda_0)\). With equality multipliers included, the corresponding slope is \((f_1(x_0),\ldots,f_m(x_0),h(x_0))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The superdifferential of a concave dual function consists of all slopes of affine functions supporting the dual function from above. It is the negative of the ordinary convex subdifferential of the negative dual function. Whenever the inner Lagrangian minimization is attained, the constraint residuals at a minimizing primal point provide such a supporting slope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^+q(\lambda_0)=\{s:q(\lambda)\le q(\lambda_0)+s^T(\lambda-\lambda_0)\ \forall\lambda\}=-\partial(-q)(\lambda_0),\quad x_0\in\arg\min_xL(x,\lambda_0)\Rightarrow c(x_0)\in\partial^+q(\lambda_0).\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using the concave-subgradient convention, the set denoted \(\partial q(\lambda_0)\) is exactly \(\partial^+q(\lambda_0)\).
The residual relation is \(-c(x_0)\in\partial(-q)(\lambda_0)\).
special_cases_latex: If q is differentiable at \(\lambda_0\), then \(\partial^+q(\lambda_0)=\{\nabla q(\lambda_0)\}\).
If the active minimizing set has several points, their residual vectors can generate multiple supporting slopes.
immediate_consequences_latex: A dual maximizer in the interior of an unconstrained effective domain satisfies \(0\in\partial^+q(\lambda^\star)\).
Residual vectors can be used as first-order information for maximizing q or minimizing \(-q\).
boundary_notes: At boundary points of the multiplier cone, dual optimality also involves the cone normal and is not simply zero supergradient.
The exact full superdifferential may require closure or convex-hull qualifications when the inner minimizer is nonunique or not attained.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(g(\lambda,\nu)=\inf_{x\in D}L(x,\lambda,\nu)\) be the dual function of a minimization problem with m inequality constraints and p equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General finite-dimensional Lagrangian dual, whether or not the primal problem is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Lagrange dual problem is \(\operatorname{maximize}_{\lambda,
u}\ g(\lambda,
u)\) subject to \(\lambda\ge0\), with \(
u\in\mathbb R^p\) unrestricted. Its value is \(d^\star=\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m,
u\in\mathbb R^p}g(\lambda,
u)\). A pair \((\lambda,
u)\) is effectively dual feasible when \(\lambda\ge0\) and \(g(\lambda,
u)>-\infty\); it is dual optimal when it is feasible and attains \(d^\star\). The problem is a convex optimization problem in the maximization convention because g is concave and the sign cone is convex. Its objective is the best lower bound on the primal value obtainable from the Lagrangian family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lagrange dual problem maximizes the concave dual function over nonnegative inequality multipliers and unrestricted equality multipliers. A multiplier is effectively feasible only when its dual-function value is not minus infinity. An optimal multiplier attains the supremum. The dual is a convex optimization problem even when the primal problem is nonconvex.

u):\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m,\ 
u\in\mathbb R^p\},\qquad (\lambda^\star,
u^\star)\in\arg\max_{\lambda\ge0,
u}g(\lambda,

The hypograph form is \(\sup\{t:t\le L(x,\lambda,\nu)\ \forall x\in D,\ \lambda\ge0\}\).

With no equalities, the dual feasible set is contained in \(\mathbb R_+^m\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Its optimal value satisfies \(d^\star\le p^\star\).

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Optimization Form of the Canonical Dual
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The canonical multiplier dual is always a convex optimization problem because it maximizes a concave function over a convex multiplier set, even for a nonconvex primal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For arbitrary functions \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_m\) and \(h\), the dual function \(g\) is concave in \((\lambda,\nu)\). Hence
\[
\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m,\,\nu\in\mathbb R^p}g(\lambda,\nu)
\]
is a convex optimization problem in the standard sense, equivalently the minimization of the convex function \(-g\) over \(\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^p\), even when the primal problem is nonconvex.
assumptions_latex: The canonical Lagrangian and dual function are defined as in the seed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is concave, and the canonical dual is equivalently \(\inf_{\lambda\geq0,\nu}[-g(\lambda,\nu)]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization geometry of the canonical multiplier dual, independent of primal convexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Multiplier Dual
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The canonical dual maximizes the Lagrangian infimum over sign-compatible multipliers. Its value is always a lower bound on the primal infimum; equality needs additional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
g(\lambda,\nu)=\inf_{x\in X}\left(f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x)+\langle\nu,h(x)\rangle\right).
\]
The canonical multiplier dual problem is
\[
\sup\{g(\lambda,\nu):\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m,\ \nu\in\mathbb R^p\}.
\]
If \(p^*\) is the primal infimum and \(d^*\) is this dual supremum, weak duality gives \(d^*\leq p^*\). Equality is not part of the construction and requires an additional constraint qualification or closedness condition.
assumptions_latex: \(m,p\in\mathbb N\), \(X\neq\varnothing\), \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to\mathbb R\), and \(h:X\to\mathbb R^p\).
The primal problem is \(\inf\{f_0(x):x\in X,\ f_i(x)\leq0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ h(x)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The canonical dual is \(\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m,\,\nu\in\mathbb R^p}g(\lambda,\nu)\), and its value does not exceed the primal infimum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard multiplier maximization and weak duality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical multiplier dual of a convex program
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. Let \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_m:C\to\mathbb R\) be convex, and let \(h(x)=Ax-b\) be affine. Consider \(\inf\{f_0(x):x\in C,\ f_i(x)\le0,\ Ax=b\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex standard form. This is the convex specialization of the general Lagrange dual problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The canonical multiplier dual is \(\sup_{\lambda\ge0,\nu\in\mathbb R^p}\inf_{x\in C}\{f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_if_i(x)+\nu^T(Ax-b)\}\). Its variables are precisely one nonnegative scalar multiplier for each scalar convex inequality and one unrestricted multiplier component for each affine equality. The extended dual objective equals \(-\infty\) whenever the inner convex minimization is unbounded below. Any algebraic conditions needed to make the inner infimum finite are implicit dual-domain constraints and may be exposed explicitly without changing the dual value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex program in standard form, the canonical multiplier dual maximizes the minimum Lagrangian value over nonnegative inequality multipliers and free equality multipliers. Finiteness conditions generated by the inner minimization are part of the dual domain, even if they are not initially written as explicit constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^\star=\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m,\nu\in\mathbb R^p}\left[\inf_{x\in C}\bigl(f_0(x)+\lambda^Tf(x)+\nu^T(Ax-b)\bigr)\right].\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: The dual may be written with the explicit constraint \((\lambda,\nu)\in\operatorname{dom}g\).
When the inner minimization yields algebraic equalities or semidefinite conditions, those conditions can replace the minus-infinity branches of g.
special_cases_latex: For a standard-form linear program, eliminating redundant multipliers yields the familiar linear-programming dual.
For a convex quadratic program, finiteness of the inner infimum produces matrix range and positive-semidefiniteness conditions.
immediate_consequences_latex: The canonical multiplier dual is a convex optimization problem.
Every feasible multiplier pair supplies a global lower bound on the convex primal value.
boundary_notes: Convexity alone does not guarantee equality of primal and dual values; a suitable constraint qualification is still needed.
Vector inequalities ordered by a cone require cone-dual rather than componentwise nonnegative multipliers.

knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchy of Partial-Dual Bounds
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nested dualized blocks, dualizing more constraints cannot improve the partial-dual lower bound; the endpoints are the primal value and the full Lagrange-dual value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(D\subseteq I\), let \(d_D\) be the partial-dual value obtained by dualizing the constraints in \(D\) while retaining those in \(I\setminus D\) in the inner minimization. If \(D_1\subseteq D_2\), then
\[
d_{D_2}\leq d_{D_1}\leq p^*.
\]
Thus retaining more constraints in the inner problem can only strengthen the Lagrangian lower bound. At the endpoints, \(d_{\varnothing}=p^*\), while \(d_I\) is the ordinary full Lagrange-dual value.
assumptions_latex: A common finite constraint index set \(I\) is partitioned into dualized indices \(D\) and retained indices \(I\setminus D\).
All selected inequality constraints use nonnegative multipliers.
\(D_1\subseteq D_2\subseteq I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{D_2}\leq d_{D_1}\leq p^*\); moreover, \(d_{\varnothing}=p^*\) and \(d_I\) is the full Lagrange-dual value.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonic comparison between partial duals formed by dualizing nested constraint blocks.

notation.meaning: partial-dual value for dualized index set \(D\)

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Lagrangian Dualization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial dualization keeps the retained constraint block inside the inner minimization and assigns multipliers only to the selected inequality block, still producing a valid lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\lambda_D\in\mathbb R_+^D\), define
\[
L_D(x,\lambda_D)=f_0(x)+\sum_{i\in D}\lambda_i f_i(x),\qquad g_D(\lambda_D)=\inf_{x\in X_R}L_D(x,\lambda_D).
\]
The partial Lagrangian dual is
\[
\sup_{\lambda_D\in\mathbb R_+^D}g_D(\lambda_D).
\]
Every \(x\in X_R\) satisfying \(f_i(x)\leq0\) for all \(i\in D\) obeys \(g_D(\lambda_D)\leq f_0(x)\), so the partial-dual value is a lower bound on the primal infimum.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite index set, \(D\subseteq I\), \(X_R\neq\varnothing\), and \(f_0,f_i:X_R\to\mathbb R\) for every \(i\in I\).
The retained constraints define \(X_R\), and the primal problem additionally imposes \(f_i(x)\leq0\) for every \(i\in D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The partial dual is \(\sup_{\lambda_D\in\mathbb R_+^D}\inf_{x\in X_R}[f_0(x)+\sum_{i\in D}\lambda_i f_i(x)]\), and its value is at most the primal infimum.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partial dualization of selected equality and inequality blocks while retaining all remaining constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X_R\) impose all retained constraints, let \(D_I\) index dualized inequalities \(f_i(x)\leq0\), and let \(D_E\) index dualized equalities \(h_j(x)=0\). Define
\[
L_D(x,\lambda,\nu)=f_0(x)+\sum_{i\in D_I}\lambda_i f_i(x)+\sum_{j\in D_E}\nu_j h_j(x),
\quad g_D(\lambda,\nu)=\inf_{x\in X_R}L_D(x,\lambda,\nu).
\]
Then
\[
\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^{D_I},\,\nu\in\mathbb R^{D_E}}g_D(\lambda,\nu)
\]
is a lower bound on the primal infimum. Dualizing every eligible constraint recovers the canonical multiplier dual; taking either selected block empty gives the equality-only or inequality-only variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial dualization may price any selected equality and inequality blocks, retaining all other constraints explicitly and preserving weak duality.
assumptions_latex: \(X_R\neq\varnothing\) is the set defined by retained constraints.
Dualized inequalities use nonnegative multipliers, while dualized equalities use unrestricted multipliers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{\lambda\geq0,\nu}g_D(\lambda,\nu)\leq p^*\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\inf\{f_0(x):x\in C,\ f_i(x)\le0\ (i\in I\cup J),\ h_k(x)=0\ (k\in E\cup F)\}\), where I and E index the constraints to be dualized and J and F index constraints retained in the inner problem.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional minimization. The retained feasible set may encode constraints chosen for structural or computational reasons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the retained set \(C_R=\{x\in C:f_j(x)\le0\  orall j\in J,\ h_k(x)=0\  orall k\in F\}\). The partial Lagrangian is \(L_{I,E}(x,\lambda_I,
u_E)=f_0(x)+\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i f_i(x)+\sum_{k\in E}
u_kh_k(x)\) for \(x\in C_R\). Its partial dual function and problem are \(g_{I,E}(\lambda_I,
u_E)=\inf_{x\in C_R}L_{I,E}(x,\lambda_I,
u_E)\) and \(\sup\{g_{I,E}(\lambda_I,
u_E):\lambda_I\ge0,
u_E\in\mathbb R^{|E|}\}\). Only the selected constraints receive multipliers; all remaining constraints continue to restrict the inner primal minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial Lagrangian dualization assigns multipliers only to a selected subset of constraints. The other constraints remain enforced in the inner minimization. The resulting partial dual maximizes the lower bounds obtained from this restricted multiplier family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(g_{I,E}(\lambda_I,
u_E)=\inf_{x\in C_R}\left(f_0(x)+\lambda_I^Tf_I(x)+
u_E^Th_E(x)ight),\qquad d_{I,E}^\star=\sup_{\lambda_I\ge0,
u_E}g_{I,E}(\lambda_I,
u_E).\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: The retained constraints can be incorporated by adding \(\delta_{C_R}(x)\) to the partial Lagrangian.
Full dualization is recovered when \(J=F=\varnothing\); no dualization is recovered when \(I=E=\varnothing\).
special_cases_latex: Lagrangian relaxation of complicating constraints retains a tractable core set C_R.
A block-separable model may dualize only coupling equalities while retaining all local constraints.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every partially dual-feasible multiplier gives a lower bound on the original primal value.
If more constraints are dualized, the resulting lower-bound family changes and need not have the same optimal value without additional regularity.
boundary_notes: Retaining a nonconvex constraint can make evaluation of the partial dual function nonconvex even though the dual function remains concave in its multipliers.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Rescaling of Inequality Constraints
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive rescaling of inequality constraints recoordinates their nonnegative multipliers and preserves the dual value and optimizer correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(s_i>0\) and replace \(f_i(x)\leq0\) by \(\widetilde f_i(x)=s_i f_i(x)\leq0\). With \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\ldots,s_m)\), the transformed dual function satisfies
\[
\widetilde g(\mu,\nu)=g(S\mu,\nu).
\]
Because \(\mu\mapsto S\mu\) is a bijection of \(\mathbb R_+^m\), the dual values and attainment status are preserved, and maximizers correspond by \(\lambda=S\mu\).
assumptions_latex: \(s_i>0\) for every inequality index.
The original and rescaled canonical dual functions are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde g(\mu,\nu)=g(S\mu,\nu)\), and the two dual problems have equal values with bijectively corresponding maximizers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value- and optimizer-preserving reparameterization of scalar inequality multipliers.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Image Criterion for a General Linear Rewriting
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general linear rewriting restricts the original dual function to the image of the transpose multiplier map; non-surjectivity need not preserve the dual value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a general linear rewriting \(\widetilde h=Sh\),
\[
\widetilde g(\mu)=g(S^{\mathsf T}\mu),\qquad
\sup_{\mu}\widetilde g(\mu)=\sup_{\nu\in\operatorname{range}S^{\mathsf T}}g(\nu).
\]
Thus invertibility is a sufficient condition for automatic invariance. If \(S^{\mathsf T}\) is not surjective, the transformed problem explores only a restricted multiplier family; its dual value equals the original one exactly when this restriction does not lower the supremum. A bijection is sufficient but not necessary for equality.
assumptions_latex: The original equality-constraint dual function is \(g(\nu)=\inf_x[\varphi(x)+\langle\nu,h(x)\rangle]\).
A linear rewriting \(\widetilde h=Sh\) has transformed multiplier \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{\mu}\widetilde g(\mu)=\sup_{\nu\in\operatorname{range}S^{\mathsf T}}g(\nu)\); equality with the original dual value holds exactly when restricting \(g\) to \(\operatorname{range}S^{\mathsf T}\) does not lower its supremum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp multiplier-image limitation for a general linear equality-constraint rewriting.

notation.meaning: multiplier image induced by the rewriting

knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent Dual Parameterizations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible linear rewriting of equality constraints applies the transpose transformation to their multipliers, preserving dual values and optimizer correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the original and transformed dual functions by
\[
g(\nu)=\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(\varphi(x)+\langle\nu,h(x)\rangle\bigr),\qquad
\widetilde g(\mu)=\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(\varphi(x)+\langle\mu,\widetilde h(x)\rangle\bigr).
\]
The systems \(h(x)=0\) and \(\widetilde h(x)=Sh(x)=0\) have the same feasible points, and
\[
\langle\mu,\widetilde h(x)\rangle=\langle S^{\mathsf T}\mu,h(x)\rangle.
\]
Consequently, \(\widetilde g(\mu)=g(S^{\mathsf T}\mu)\). Since \(\mu\mapsto S^{\mathsf T}\mu\) is bijective,
\[
\sup_{\mu\in\mathbb R^p}\widetilde g(\mu)=\sup_{\nu\in\mathbb R^p}g(\nu),
\]
and maximizers correspond by \(\nu=S^{\mathsf T}\mu\).
assumptions_latex: \(p\in\mathbb N\), \(X\neq\varnothing\), \(\varphi:X\to\mathbb R\), and \(h:X\to\mathbb R^p\).
\(S\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}\) is invertible, and \(\widetilde h(x)=Sh(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde g(\mu)=g(S^{\mathsf T}\mu)\), so the two dual problems have identical values and corresponding maximizers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invertible linear reparameterization of equality multipliers.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rectangular extension of invertible equality-residual reparameterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^q\) be injective and \(\widetilde h=Sh\). Then \(h(x)=0\) if and only if \(\widetilde h(x)=0\), and \(\widetilde g(\mu)=g(S^{\mathsf T}\mu)\). Because \(S^{\mathsf T}\) is surjective, \(\sup_\mu\widetilde g(\mu)=\sup_\nu g(\nu)\), and transformed maximizers are the inverse images under \(S^{\mathsf T}\) of original maximizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An injective rectangular encoding of equality residuals preserves feasibility and the optimized dual value, though transformed optimal multipliers may be nonunique.
assumptions_latex: \(S:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^q\) is injective.
The dual functions are interpreted in the extended-real sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde g=g\circ S^{\mathsf T}\) and \(\sup\widetilde g=\sup g\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent linear reparameterization of a cone-valued inequality residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq Y\) be a closed convex cone and let \(S:Y\to Y\) be invertible with \(S(K)=K\). Then \(G(x)\in-K\) if and only if \(SG(x)\in-K\). For \(g(y)=\inf_x[f_0(x)+\langle y,G(x)\rangle]\) and \(\widetilde g(\mu)=\inf_x[f_0(x)+\langle\mu,SG(x)\rangle]\), one has \(\widetilde g(\mu)=g(S^{\mathsf T}\mu)\). Moreover, \(S^{\mathsf T}\) maps \(K^*\) bijectively onto \(K^*\), so the optimized dual values and optimizer sets correspond.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone automorphism preserves the generalized inequality and transports its dual multipliers by the adjoint without changing the dual value.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
\(S\) is invertible and \(S(K)=K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{\mu\in K^*}\widetilde g(\mu)=\sup_{y\in K^*}g(y)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for value preservation by linear equality-residual transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A noninjective residual map can discard constraints and restrict accessible original multipliers.
assumptions_latex: \(S:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^q\) is linear.
\(g\) and \(\widetilde g\) are the equality-multiplier dual functions for \(h\) and \(Sh\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup\widetilde g=\sup_{\nu\in\operatorname{range}S^{\mathsf T}}g(\nu)\leq\sup g\), with equality not guaranteed.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let two dual formulations be \(\sup_{y\in Y}g(y)\) and \(\sup_{z\in Z}\tilde g(z)\), where minus-infinity values encode implicit infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional dual formulations. Equivalence concerns feasible lower bounds and objective values, not merely equality of optimal values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The two dual formulations are equivalent parameterizations when there are maps \(T:Y_{\mathrm f}\to Z_{\mathrm f}\) and \(S:Z_{\mathrm f}\to Y_{\mathrm f}\) such that \(S\circ T\) and \(T\circ S\) are identity maps on the effective feasible sets and \(\tilde g(Ty)=g(y)\) for every \(y\in Y_{\mathrm f}\). More generally, elimination equivalence permits many-to-one maps provided every feasible point in either formulation has an objective-preserving representative in the other. Typical operations are exposing implicit finiteness conditions as explicit constraints, eliminating a multiplier determined by an affine equality, applying an invertible affine change of dual variables, or reversing multiplier signs together with the corresponding constraint convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two duals are equivalent parameterizations when their effective feasible points correspond in an objective-preserving way. A one-to-one change of variables is the cleanest case, but eliminating redundant multipliers is also allowed if every lower bound represented by one formulation has an equal-valued representative in the other. Merely sharing the same optimal value is weaker than parameterization equivalence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(Y_{\mathrm f})=Z_{\mathrm f},\qquad \tilde g(Ty)=g(y)\ \forall y\in Y_{\mathrm f},\qquad \sup_{y\in Y_{\mathrm f}}g(y)=\sup_{z\in Z_{\mathrm f}}\tilde g(z).\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: An extended-valued objective with \(g(y)=-\infty\) off an affine set is equivalent to maximizing its finite formula subject to that affine set explicitly.
If \(T\) is an affine bijection, the optimizer sets correspond as \(\operatorname{argmax}\tilde g=T(\operatorname{argmax}g)\).
special_cases_latex: In a linear-programming dual, an equality can determine a nonnegative slack multiplier, which can then be eliminated to obtain an inequality form.
The conventions \(Ax=b\) with multiplier \(\nu\) and \(b-Ax=0\) with multiplier \(-\nu\) are equivalent.
immediate_consequences_latex: Equivalent parameterizations have identical dual values and attainability behavior under a bijective correspondence.
Certificates can be transported through the parameter map.
boundary_notes: Equality of optimal values alone does not establish equivalence of feasible lower-bound families.
A noninvertible scaling or sign change can alter cone feasibility and must be checked explicitly.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonbijective Rewritings Need Not Preserve the Dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp limitation of value-preserving multiplier reparameterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Preservation by a constraint transformation follows from a bijection of the admissible multiplier sets that leaves every Lagrangian slice unchanged. If the induced multiplier map is not bijective—such as a singular rewriting that deletes constraint directions—this argument fails: the transformed feasible set or the family of Lagrangian lower bounds may change, so equality of dual values and correspondence of maximizers are not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Only transformations inducing a bijection of admissible multipliers automatically preserve the dual; singular or direction-deleting rewritings need not do so.
assumptions_latex: A proposed constraint rewriting induces a linear map between multiplier spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without a bijection of admissible multiplier sets preserving Lagrangian slices, dual-value and optimizer invariance cannot be concluded.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perturbational-conjugate duality generated by a convex bifunction
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(U=\mathbb R^m\), \(X=\mathbb R^n\), and let \(F:U\times X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a proper convex perturbation function. The unperturbed primal problem is \(\inf_xF(0,x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex perturbation theory. Closedness is not required to define the pair, but it governs biconjugacy and strong-duality conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The perturbational-conjugate duality family generated by F consists of the marginal value function \(p(u)=\inf_{x\in X}F(u,x)\), the Lagrangian \(L(u^*,x)=\inf_{u\in U}\{F(u,x)+\langle u^*,u\rangle\}\), and the dual objective \(d(u^*)=\inf_xL(u^*,x)=\inf_u\{p(u)+\langle u^*,u\rangle\}=-p^*(-u^*)=-F^*(-u^*,0)\). Its primal and dual problems are \(p(0)=\inf_xF(0,x)\) and \(\sup_{u^*\in U^*}d(u^*)\), respectively. Every choice of a perturbation representation F for the same unperturbed objective can generate a different member of this duality family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex perturbation function produces a value function by minimizing over the primal variable. Conjugating that value function in the perturbation variable yields a concave dual objective. Equivalently, one first forms a Lagrangian by minimizing the perturbation function plus a linear perturbation price, and then minimizes over the primal variable. The chosen perturbation model is part of the dual construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(u)=\inf_xF(u,x),\quad L(u^*,x)=\inf_u\{F(u,x)+\langle u^*,u\rangle\},\quad d(u^*)=-p^*(-u^*)=-F^*(-u^*,0),\quad \sup_{u^*}d(u^*)\le p(0).\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: With \(y=-u^*\), the dual is \(\sup_y\{-p^*(y)\}=\sup_y\{-F^*(y,0)\}\).
The adjoint-bifunction formulation identifies the dual objective with the zero-perturbation slice of the concave adjoint of F.
special_cases_latex: Right-hand-side perturbations of ordinary constraints recover the Lagrange multiplier dual.
Choosing \(F(u,x)=f(x)+\delta_{\{Ax-b=u\}}(u)\) produces an equality-constrained conjugate dual.
immediate_consequences_latex: Fenchel's inequality yields weak duality for every \(u^*\).
Different perturbation maps can give different dual feasible sets even when \(F(0,\cdot)\) is unchanged.
boundary_notes: The marginal p need not be closed even when F is closed.
Zero duality gap and dual attainment require regularity beyond proper convexity.

convex conjugate on the product space
