knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex perturbation model and its value function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let U and X be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(0\in U\) denote the reference perturbation, and let \(F:U\times X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real minimization. Convex perturbation theory assumes joint convexity of F, not merely convexity of each isolated slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A perturbation-function framework for the unperturbed objective \(x\mapsto F(0,x)\) is the family of perturbed problems \(P_u:\inf_{x\in X}F(u,x)\), indexed by \(u\in U\), together with the marginal value function \(p:U\to\mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\}\), \(p(u)=\inf_{x\in X}F(u,x)\). The unperturbed primal value is \(p(0)\). The effective perturbation domain is \(\operatorname{dom}p=\{u:p(u)<+\infty\}\); infeasible perturbations have value \(+\infty\), while value \(-\infty\) records unboundedness below. The framework is convex when F is jointly convex on \(U\times X\), in which case p is convex whenever it is not identically minus infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perturbation framework embeds one optimization problem into a family indexed by a perturbation vector. The joint extended-valued function specifies both costs and feasibility. Minimizing it over the decision variable gives the value function, and the value at zero is the original primal value. Positive infinity records infeasibility and minus infinity records unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_u:\ p(u)=\inf_{x\in X}F(u,x),\qquad p(0)=\inf_{x\in X}F(0,x),\qquad \operatorname{dom}p=\{u:p(u)<+\infty\}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \((Fu)(x)=F(u,x)\), the value function is Rockafellar's marginal \((\inf F)(u)=\inf_x(Fu)(x)\).
A family of feasible sets \(S(u)\) and costs \(f(u,x)\) is represented by \(F(u,x)=f(u,x)+\delta_{S(u)}(x)\).
special_cases_latex: For perturbed inequalities \(f_i(x)\le u_i\) and equalities \(h(x)=v\), the value function is the optimal cost as a function of \((u,v)\).
A pure objective perturbation has \(F(u,x)=f(x)+\psi(u,x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Joint convexity of F makes the marginal value function convex, subject to the usual properness convention.
The local stability of the primal value can be studied through p near zero.
boundary_notes: Separate convexity in u and x is insufficient for the standard joint-convex perturbation framework.
The infimum defining p need not be attained, and p need not be lower semicontinuous.

knowledge_statements.title: Dependence on the Chosen Perturbation Model
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two proper convex perturbation models can agree at the reference parameter yet yield different dual bounds, so the dual is not intrinsic to the unperturbed objective alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define two proper convex perturbation functions on \(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\) by \[F_1(x,u)=1+\delta_{\{0\}}(x)\] and \[F_2(x,u)=\delta_{\{0\}}(x)+q(u),\qquad q(u)=\begin{cases}+\infty,&u<0,\\1,&u=0,\\0,&u>0.\end{cases}\] Both satisfy \(F_1(x,0)=F_2(x,0)=1+\delta_{\{0\}}(x)\), so their common primal value is \(p=1\). Their value functions are \(v_1\equiv1\) and \(v_2=q\), and their perturbational dual values are \[\sup_y\{-v_1^*(y)\}=1,\qquad \sup_y\{-v_2^*(y)\}=0.\] Thus the perturbational dual value is determined by the full perturbation model, not by the unperturbed primal problem alone.
assumptions_latex: X=\mathbb{R}
U=\mathbb{R}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_x F_1(x,0)=\inf_x F_2(x,0)=1,\qquad d_1=1\ne 0=d_2
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional example showing that the perturbational dual depends on the chosen off-reference extension even when the reference primal objective is identical.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Perturbation Models
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function of a decision and perturbation parameter defines a family of optimization problems; setting the parameter to zero recovers the primal problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(U\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces. A primal perturbation model is a proper convex function \(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). For each parameter \(u\in U\), the associated problem is \(P(u):\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u)\). The original, unperturbed primal problem is \(P(0)\), and its value is \[p:=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,0).\] The dependence on \(u\) records admissible perturbations used to construct a conjugate dual problem.

F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perturbation function and its marginal value representation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:U\times X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a proper convex function on finite-dimensional spaces and let \(p(u)=\inf_xF(u,x)\). Define \(F^*(u^*,x^*)=\sup_{u,x}\{\langle u^*,u\rangle+\langle x^*,x\rangle-F(u,x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex marginalization. The identities are extended-real identities and do not assert attainment of the marginal infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A value-marginal representation pair is a pair \((F,p)\) satisfying \(p(u)=\inf_{x\in X}F(u,x)\) for every \(u\in U\). The function F is the joint perturbation representation and p is its marginal value function. Their conjugates obey \(p^*(u^*)=F^*(u^*,0)\). Hence the unperturbed primal value is the distinguished marginal value \(p(0)=\inf_xF(0,x)\), while dual affine minorants of p are encoded by the zero-primal-dual slice of \(F^*\). The pair retains more information than p alone because different joint functions F can have the same marginal p but different minimizer mappings and perturbation structures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value-marginal pair consists of a joint perturbation function and the value function obtained by minimizing out the decision variable. The conjugate of the marginal is the restriction of the joint conjugate to zero in the dual coordinate corresponding to the eliminated decision variable. The joint representation contains information that the value function alone does not retain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(u)=\inf_xF(u,x)\ \forall u,\qquad p(0)=\inf_xF(0,x),\qquad p^*(u^*)=F^*(u^*,0).\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: The epigraph of p is the smallest upward-closed set containing the projection of \(\operatorname{epi}F\) onto \(U\times\mathbb R\); closure may be needed at unattained boundary values.
The identity \(p^*(u^*)=\sup_{u,x}\{\langle u^*,u\rangle-F(u,x)\}\) is the product-space form of the conjugate relation.
special_cases_latex: If \(F(u,x)=f(x)+\delta_{\{Ax-b=u\}}(u)\), then p is the right-hand-side value function.
If X is a singleton, marginalization is trivial and p is the corresponding slice of F.
immediate_consequences_latex: The perturbational dual objective can be written as \(-p^*(-u^*)=-F^*(-u^*,0)\).
Subgradients of p at zero represent supporting perturbation prices when p is proper there.
boundary_notes: Projection of a closed convex epigraph need not be closed, so p can fail to be lower semicontinuous.
The marginal representation is not unique.

zero primal-dual slice of the joint conjugate

knowledge_statements.title: Value-Function Representations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The value function minimizes the perturbation function over decisions. Projecting the perturbation epigraph gives the value epigraph except that boundary points may be missing when the infimum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(U\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, and let \(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. knowledge_statements.title: Marginal-Function Representations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The marginal function is obtained by taking the infimum over the decision coordinate. It may equal negative infinity, and its effective domain is the parameter projection of the perturbation function's domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(U\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, and let \(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. Its marginal with respect to \(X\) is the function \(v:U\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) defined by \[v(u):=\bigl(\inf\nolimits_XF\bigr)(u):=\inf\{F(x,u):x\in X\}.\] With \(\operatorname{dom}v:=\{u\in U:v(u)<+\infty\}\), one has \[\operatorname{dom}v=\operatorname{proj}_U(\operatorname{dom}F).\] Thus marginalization removes the decision coordinate by infimal projection. When the infimum is finite and attained at \(u\), its minimizing decisions are exactly \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}F(x,u)\).

F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v=\inf\nolimits_XF,\qquad \operatorname{dom}v=\operatorname{proj}_U(\operatorname{dom}F)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marginalization means infimal projection over the decision coordinate and may produce the value negative infinity.

knowledge_statements.title: Value–Marginal Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The value function is the marginal of the perturbation function, and its conjugate equals the perturbation conjugate restricted to zero decision-dual coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v(u):=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u)\). For every \(y\in U\), conjugation of the marginal gives \[v^*(y)=\sup_{u\in U}\{\langle y,u\rangle-v(u)\}=\sup_{(x,u)\in X\times U}\{\langle y,u\rangle-F(x,u)\}=F^*(0,y).\] Hence the value-function representation and marginal-function representation describe the same object, while its conjugate is obtained by restricting the full conjugate of \(F\) to zero decision-space dual coordinate.

F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v=\inf\nolimits_XF,\qquad v^*(y)=F^*(0,y)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate dual of a perturbation value function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:U\times X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a proper convex perturbation function, let \(p(u)=\inf_xF(u,x)\), and take the unperturbed primal value to be \(p(0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex perturbation duality. The sign convention uses the perturbation-price term \(+\langle u^*,u\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The perturbational dual objective is \(d(u^*)=\inf_{u\in U}\{p(u)+\langle u^*,u\rangle\}=-p^*(-u^*)=-F^*(-u^*,0)\). The perturbational dual problem is \(d^\star=\sup_{u^*\in U^*}d(u^*)\). Its effective feasible set is \(\{u^*:p^*(-u^*)<+\infty\}\). For every \(u^*\), the value at \(u=0\) gives \(d(u^*)\le p(0)\), so \(d^\star\le p(0)\). A dual optimizer is a perturbation price \(u^{*\star}\) attaining this supremum. Under the alternative variable \(y=-u^*\), the same problem is \(\sup_y\{-p^*(y)\}=\sup_y\{-F^*(y,0)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The perturbational dual maximizes the negative conjugate of the perturbation value function. With the chosen sign convention, a dual variable prices perturbations through a positive inner-product term. The effective dual domain consists of prices where the conjugate is finite. Every such dual value is bounded above by the unperturbed primal value. Reversing the sign of the dual variable gives the commonly used negative-conjugate form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^\star=\sup_{u^*\in U^*}\left[-p^*(-u^*)\right]=\sup_{u^*\in U^*}\left[-F^*(-u^*,0)\right]\le p(0).\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: Setting \(y=-u^*\) gives \(d^\star=\sup_y\{-p^*(y)\}\).
The nested form is \(d^\star=\sup_{u^*}\inf_{u,x}\{F(u,x)+\langle u^*,u\rangle\}\).
special_cases_latex: For right-hand-side constraint perturbations, this dual is the ordinary Lagrange multiplier dual after the corresponding sign identification.
If p is closed and convex, the dual value is \(p^{**}(0)=p(0)\), though attainment of the supremum is separate.
immediate_consequences_latex: Weak duality holds without a constraint qualification.
A dual optimum, when attained with equality of values, supplies a global affine support of p at zero.
boundary_notes: If p is not closed at zero, the dual value can equal its lower-semicontinuous convex closure at zero rather than p(0).
The sign of the multiplier depends on whether perturbations enter as relaxed right-hand sides or residuals.

notation.meaning: convex conjugate of the value function

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Attainment and Supporting-Subgradient Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter-space dual maximizer is exactly a supporting subgradient of the closed value function at zero; under no gap it is exactly a subgradient of the original value function there.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v:U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex on a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and suppose \(v^{**}(0)\) is finite. A vector \(\bar y\in U\) attains \[\sup_{y\in U}\{-v^*(y)\}=v^{**}(0)\] if and only if \[v^{**}(0)+v^*(\bar y)=0,\] equivalently \(\bar y\in\partial v^{**}(0)\). Consequently, the dual maximum is attained exactly when \(\partial v^{**}(0)\ne\varnothing\). If there is no gap, \(v(0)=v^{**}(0)\), then the dual maximizers are exactly \(\partial v(0)\). Thus equality of primal and dual values alone does not imply dual attainment; a supporting subgradient at the reference parameter is additionally required.
assumptions_latex: U=\mathbb{R}^m
v:U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
v^{**}(0)\in\mathbb{R}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in U}\{-v^*(y)\}=\partial v^{**}(0),\qquad v(0)=v^{**}(0)\Longrightarrow \operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in U}\{-v^*(y)\}=\partial v(0)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional dual-attainment certificate for the perturbational dual, separating equality of values from existence of a dual maximizer.

notation.meaning: Fenchel biconjugate of the perturbation value function

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Space Dualization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing only the perturbation parameter evaluates the biconjugate of the value function at zero, giving a lower bound on the primal value and equality when the proper convex value function is lower semicontinuous there.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(U\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and define \(v(u):=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u)\). Parameter-space dualization gives \[d:=\sup_{y\in U}\{-F^*(0,y)\}=\sup_{y\in U}\{-v^*(y)\}=v^{**}(0).\] Hence weak duality is \[d\le v(0)=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,0)=:p.\] If \(v\) is proper and lower semicontinuous at \(0\), then \(v^{**}(0)=v(0)\), and therefore \(d=p\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional perturbational duality for an extended-real convex bifunction. The distinguished parameter is \(u=0\); neither strong duality nor attainment is included in the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[v_P:=p(0)=\inf_{x\in X}F(0,x),\qquad d(u^*):=\inf_{u\in U}\{p(u)+\langle u^*,u\rangle\}=-p^*(-u^*).\] The parameter-space dual problem associated with \(F\) is \[v_D:=\sup_{u^*\in U^*}d(u^*)=\sup_{u^*\in U^*}\inf_{(u,x)\in U\times X}\{F(u,x)+\langle u^*,u\rangle\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a perturbation bifunction \(F(u,x)\), partially minimize over the decision variable to obtain the value function \(p(u)=\inf_xF(u,x)\). The primal value is \(p(0)\). A parameter-space dual variable \(u^*\) prices the perturbation, giving \(d(u^*)=\inf_u[p(u)+\langle u^*,u\rangle]=-p^*(-u^*)\); maximizing this function defines the dual problem.

immediate_consequences_latex: The choice \(u=0\) gives \(d(u^*)\leq p(0)\) for every \(u^*\), hence the construction always satisfies weak duality.
boundary_notes: The definition does not assert that \(p\) is closed at \(0\), that \(v_D=v_P\), or that either extremum is attained.

knowledge_statements.title: Slice-Wise Partial-Conjugation Inversion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative partial conjugation reconstructs the biconjugate of each proper convex perturbation slice and reconstructs the slice itself when it is lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(x\in X\), write \(F_x(u)=F(x,u)\), and define \(L(x,y)=\inf_{u\in U}\{F_x(u)-\langle y,u\rangle\}=-F_x^*(y)\). If \(F_x\) is proper and convex, then
\[
\sup_{y\in U}\{L(x,y)+\langle y,u\rangle\}=F_x^{**}(u).
\]
Consequently, if \(F_x\) is also lower semicontinuous, then
\[
F(x,u)=\sup_{y\in U}\{L(x,y)+\langle y,u\rangle\}.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(U\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
For the fixed \(x\), \(F_x=F(x,\cdot)\) is proper and convex.
Exact recovery additionally assumes that \(F_x\) is lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{y\in U}\{L(x,y)+\langle y,u\rangle\}=F_x^{**}(u),\quad\text{and this equals }F(x,u)\text{ when }F_x\text{ is lower semicontinuous}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel–Moreau reconstruction of a perturbation slice from its negative partial conjugate.

notation.meaning: negative partial conjugate in the perturbation coordinate

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Conjugation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, partially conjugating the perturbation coordinate produces a convex-concave Lagrangian whose supremum-infimum value is the perturbational dual value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(U\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, and let \(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. Define the negative partial conjugate in the parameter coordinate by \[L(x,y):=\inf_{u\in U}\{F(x,u)-\langle y,u\rangle\},\qquad (x,y)\in X\times U.\] Then \(L\) is convex in \(x\) and concave in \(y\), and \[\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)=-F^*(0,y),\qquad y\in U.\] Consequently, \[\sup_{y\in U}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)=\sup_{y\in U}\{-F^*(0,y)\}.\]
assumptions_latex: X=\mathbb{R}^n,\quad U=\mathbb{R}^m
F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{y\in U}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)=\sup_{y\in U}\{-F^*(0,y)\}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partial conjugation in the perturbation coordinate produces the Lagrangian representation in finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Perturbation Hulls
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, the perturbational dual evaluates the lower-semicontinuous convex hull of the proper convex value function at zero, and the duality gap is its failure to agree with the original value there.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and let \(v:U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. Its lower-semicontinuous convex hull satisfies \[\operatorname{cl}v=v^{**}.\] If \(p:=v(0)\) is the primal value and \(d:=\sup_{y\in U}\{-v^*(y)\}\) is the perturbational dual value, then \[d=v^{**}(0)\le v(0)=p.\] Whenever both values are finite, the duality gap is \(v(0)-v^{**}(0)\), and strong duality holds exactly when \(v(0)=v^{**}(0)\).
assumptions_latex: U=\mathbb{R}^m
v:U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cl}v=v^{**},\qquad d=v^{**}(0)\le v(0)=p
knowledge_statements.scope_note: In finite dimensions, the dual value evaluates the lower-semicontinuous convex hull of the proper convex perturbation value function.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \[U=\mathbb R^m,\qquad p:U\to(-\infty,+\infty],\qquad p\not\equiv +\infty,\qquad p\text{ has an affine minorant}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed-convex regularization of a possibly nonclosed or nonconvex perturbation value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The closed perturbation hull of \(p\) is the function \(\overline{\operatorname{co}}p\) determined by \[\operatorname{epi}(\overline{\operatorname{co}}p)=\overline{\operatorname{co}}\bigl(\operatorname{epi}p\bigr).\] Equivalently, \[\overline{\operatorname{co}}p=p^{**}=\sup\{a:a\text{ is continuous affine and }a\leq p\}.\] It is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function majorized by \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perturbation hull replaces the epigraph of a perturbation value function by its closed convex hull. Its value function is \(\overline{\operatorname{co}}p=p^{**}\), equivalently the pointwise supremum of all continuous affine minorants of \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\overline{\operatorname{co}}p:=p^{**},\qquad \operatorname{epi}(\overline{\operatorname{co}}p)=\overline{\operatorname{co}}(\operatorname{epi}p).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[(\overline{\operatorname{co}}p)(u)=\sup\{\langle u^*,u\rangle-\alpha:\langle u^*,v\rangle-\alpha\leq p(v)\ \forall v\in U\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(p\) is convex, then \(\overline{\operatorname{co}}p=\operatorname{cl}p\).
If \(p\) is already proper, closed, and convex, then \(\overline{\operatorname{co}}p=p\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Conjugate dualization cannot distinguish \(p\) from its closed convex hull because \(p^*=(\overline{\operatorname{co}}p)^*\).
boundary_notes: If \(p\) has no affine minorant, its biconjugate may be identically \(-\infty\), so the proper-hull interpretation degenerates.
Closing only \(\operatorname{epi}p\) suffices when \(p\) is convex; convexification is additionally required for a nonconvex perturbation function.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \[f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty],\qquad g:\mathbb R^n\to[-\infty,+\infty),\] \[f^*(y)=\sup_x\{\langle y,x\rangle-f(x)\},\qquad g^*(y)=\inf_x\{\langle y,x\rangle-g(x)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex–concave Fenchel construction. Equality of optimal values and attainment require additional qualification conditions and are not part of the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper convex function \(f\) and a proper concave function \(g\), the Fenchel primal–dual pair is \[(P)\quad \inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{f(x)-g(x)\},\qquad (D)\quad \sup_{y\in\mathbb R^n}\{g^*(y)-f^*(y)\}.\] The effective feasible domains are respectively \(\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\) and \(\operatorname{dom}f^*\cap\operatorname{dom}g^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Fenchel dual construction pairs minimization of the convex difference \(f-g\) with maximization of the difference of the concave and convex conjugates, \(g^*-f^*\), using the same dual vector in both conjugates.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(h=-g\), the pair becomes \(\inf_x[f(x)+h(x)]\) and \(\sup_y[-f^*(y)-h^*(-y)]\).
special_cases_latex: For a convex set \(C\), taking \(g=-\delta_C\) gives the constrained primal \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Fenchel inequalities give \(g^*(y)-f^*(y)\leq f(x)-g(x)\) for every primal–dual feasible pair \((x,y)\).
boundary_notes: The construction alone does not imply zero duality gap.
The concave-conjugate convention for \(g^*\) differs from applying the convex conjugate directly to \(g\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel Dual of a Sum with Linear Composition
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \[X=\mathbb R^n,\quad Y=\mathbb R^m,\quad A:X\to Y\text{ linear},\quad f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty],\quad h:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty].\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional proper-convex sum–composition model. The definition specifies the primal and formal Fenchel dual but does not impose a constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sum–composition primal \[(P)\quad \inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+h(Ax)\}\] is assigned the Fenchel dual \[(D)\quad \sup_{y\in Y}\{-f^*(-A^*y)-h^*(y)\}.\] It is obtained from the perturbation \(F(u,x)=f(x)+h(Ax+u)\), whose value function is \(p(u)=\inf_xF(u,x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the objective formed by adding \(f(x)\) to the composition \(h(Ax)\), the canonical Fenchel dual maximizes \(-f^*(-A^*y)-h^*(y)\). The adjoint \(A^*\) transfers the dual variable from the range space of \(A\) to the domain space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{Dual}\bigl(\inf_x f(x)+h(Ax)\bigr)=\sup_y\{-f^*(-A^*y)-h^*(y)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Introducing \(z=Ax\), the primal is \(\inf_{x,z}\{f(x)+h(z):Ax-z=0\}\), and dualizing the equality gives the same dual objective.
special_cases_latex: For \(A=I\), the pair is \(\inf_x[f(x)+h(x)]\) and \(\sup_y[-f^*(-y)-h^*(y)]\).
For \(h=\delta_C\), the primal is \(\inf\{f(x):Ax\in C\}\) and \(h^*=\sigma_C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For all \(x\) and \(y\), \(-f^*(-A^*y)-h^*(y)\leq f(x)+h(Ax)\).
boundary_notes: A relative-interior or continuity qualification is normally required to identify the two optimal values and ensure dual attainment.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, the topology and the continuous dual must be specified explicitly.

knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel-Equality Certificate for a Linear-Composite Pair
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two compatible Fenchel–Young equalities, one transported through the adjoint, exactly characterize finite zero gap and certify primal-dual optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite primal-dual pair \((\bar x,\bar y^*)\), equality
\[
f(\bar x)+g(A\bar x)=-f^*(-A^*\bar y^*)-g^*(\bar y^*)
\]
holds if and only if
\[
-A^*\bar y^*\in\partial f(\bar x),\qquad \bar y^*\in\partial g(A\bar x).
\]
When these inclusions hold, \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y^*\) are respectively primal and dual optimal and the duality gap is zero.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper convex functions.
\(f(\bar x),g(A\bar x),f^*(-A^*\bar y^*)\), and \(g^*(\bar y^*)\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-A^*\bar y^*\in\partial f(\bar x)\) and \(\bar y^*\in\partial g(A\bar x)\) if and only if the finite primal-dual gap at \((\bar x,\bar y^*)\) is zero.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise zero-gap certificate intrinsic to the linear-composite Fenchel pair.

knowledge_statements.title: Unconditional Weak Duality for Linear Compositions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel inequalities give weak duality for every linear-composite primal-dual pair; regularity is needed only for equality or attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in X\) and \(y^*\in Y^*\),
\[
-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\le f(x)+g(Ax).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\sup_{y^*}\{-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\}\le\inf_x\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}
\]
without any relative-interior or other constraint qualification.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper convex functions.
\(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-duality component of the linear-composite construction, independent of regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Composition Dual Constructions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a linearly composed convex term, the adjoint transports the dual variable into the conjugate of the other summand; qualification yields equality and attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and let \(f\) and \(g\) be proper convex functions on \(X\) and \(Y\), respectively. If \(A(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f))\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\ne\varnothing\), then, for finite primal value, \[\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}=\max_{y\in Y}\{-f^*(-A^*y)-g^*(y)\}.\]

A:X\to Y\text{ is linear}
A(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f))\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\ne\varnothing

knowledge_statements.title: Sum–Composition Coupling
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perturbing the argument of the composed term produces one model whose restricted conjugate yields both sum and linear-composition Fenchel duals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For proper convex \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and linear \(A:X\to Y\), define \[F(x,u):=f(x)+g(Ax-u).\] Then \(F(x,0)=f(x)+g(Ax)\), and direct conjugation gives \[F^*(0,y)=f^*(A^*y)+g^*(-y).\] Hence the parameter-space dual is \[\sup_{y\in Y}\{-f^*(A^*y)-g^*(-y)\}.\] Taking \(A\) to be the identity recovers the sum construction after a change of dual-variable sign.
assumptions_latex: f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty],\ g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ are proper convex}
A:X\to Y\text{ is linear}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(x,u)=f(x)+g(Ax-u),\qquad F^*(0,y)=f^*(A^*y)+g^*(-y)

knowledge_statements.title: Essential-Closure Example for Linear Composition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex epigraph with a nonclosed projection yields a linear precomposition whose raw adjoint infimal image misses a boundary point recovered by closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2:a>0,\ b\ge1/a\},\qquad g=\sigma_C,
\]
and let \(A:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2\) be \(Ax=(x,0)\). Then \(g^*=\delta_C\) and
\[
q(s)=\inf\{g^*(s,t):t\in\mathbb R\}=\delta_{(0,+\infty)}(s).
\]
On the other hand, \((g\circ A)(x)=\delta_{(-\infty,0]}(x)\), hence
\[
(g\circ A)^*(s)=\delta_{[0,+\infty)}(s)=\operatorname{cl}q(s)\ne q(s).
\]
assumptions_latex: \(C=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2:a>0,\ b\ge1/a\}\), which is a nonempty closed convex set.
\(g=\sigma_C\) and \(A:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2\) is \(Ax=(x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q=\delta_{(0,+\infty)}\) while \((g\circ A)^*=\delta_{[0,+\infty)}=\operatorname{cl}q\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional witness showing that closure in the adjoint infimal-image formula can be essential.

notation.meaning: support function of the closed convex set

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Composition Closure and Attainment Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugating a linear precomposition generally produces the closure of an adjoint-constrained infimal image; range regularity is needed for an exact attained formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
q(x^*)=\inf\{g^*(y^*):A^*y^*=x^*\}.
\]
In general,
\[
(g\circ A)^*=\operatorname{cl}q.
\]
Without a range/domain qualification such as \(\operatorname{range}A\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\ne\varnothing\), the closure cannot generally be removed and the infimum defining \(q\) need not be attained. Under that qualification, the unclosed equality holds and the infimum is attained wherever \((g\circ A)^*\) is finite.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
\(g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and \(g\circ A\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((g\circ A)^*=\operatorname{cl}q\), where \(q(x^*)=\inf_{A^*y^*=x^*}g^*(y^*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure and attainment boundary for the linear-composition member of the parent construction family.

notation.meaning: adjoint-constrained infimal image of the conjugate

knowledge_statements.title: Construction Validity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions in finite dimensions, the conjugate of a sum is generally the lower-semicontinuous hull of the infimal convolution of the conjugates. Without relative-interior qualification, closure may be essential and attainment may fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, and let \(f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions. In general, \[(f+g)^*=\operatorname{cl}(f^*\square g^*),\qquad (f^*\square g^*)(z):=\inf_{y\in X}\{f^*(y)+g^*(z-y)\}.\] When \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)=\varnothing\), the closure can be essential, and the infimum defining the infimal convolution can fail to be attained. Thus absence of the qualification does not justify an unclosed conjugacy formula or dual attainment.
assumptions_latex: X=\mathbb{R}^n
f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (f+g)^*=\operatorname{cl}(f^*\square g^*)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional validity boundary: closure and nonattainment can occur when the relative-interior qualification is absent.

knowledge_statements.title: Infimal-Convolution Duals
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, infimal convolution minimizes over all decompositions of an argument, and Fenchel conjugation transforms it exactly into the pointwise sum of the conjugates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, and let \(f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper extended-real functions. Their infimal convolution is \[(f\square g)(x):=\inf_{z\in X}\{f(z)+g(x-z)\},\qquad x\in X.\] Its Fenchel conjugate satisfies the exact identity \[(f\square g)^*(y)=f^*(y)+g^*(y),\qquad y\in X.\] Thus marginalization over decompositions of a primal argument becomes pointwise addition in the conjugate domain. Closure issues instead arise in the reverse-direction formula for the conjugate of a sum.
assumptions_latex: X=\mathbb{R}^n
f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ are proper extended-real functions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (f\square g)^*=f^*+g^*
knowledge_statements.scope_note: In a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, conjugation converts infimal convolution exactly into pointwise addition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate linking an attained infimal-convolution decomposition to an attained conjugate-side dual variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h=f\square g\), and suppose \(z\) attains the infimum at \(x\), so \(h(x)=f(z)+g(x-z)\). For \(y\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[
y\in\partial f(z)\cap\partial g(x-z)
\]
is equivalent to
\[
f(z)+g(x-z)+f^*(y)+g^*(y)=\langle y,x\rangle.
\]
Whenever these conditions hold, \(y\in\partial h(x)\), and \(y\) attains
\[
\sup_u\{\langle u,x\rangle-f^*(u)-g^*(u)\}=h(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An attained decomposition and a common subgradient certify simultaneous primal decomposition optimality, dual attainment, and absence of a closure gap at the point.
assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper convex functions.
\(z\) attains \((f\square g)(x)\).
The displayed primal values are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The common-subgradient condition is equivalent to the displayed Fenchel equality and certifies \(y\in\partial(f\square g)(x)\) and dual attainment at value \((f\square g)(x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proper Inputs Need Not Give a Proper Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp propriety failure for infimal convolution even with finite closed convex operands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(\mathbb R\), let \(f(z)=z\) and \(g(w)=0\). Both functions are finite, proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, but
\[
(f\square g)(x)=\inf_{z\in\mathbb R}\{z+0\}=-\infty
\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R.
\]
Thus properness, closedness, and convexity of the operands do not ensure that their infimal convolution is proper.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two finite closed convex functions can have an infimal convolution equal to minus infinity everywhere.
assumptions_latex: \(f(z)=z\) and \(g(w)=0\) on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f\square g)(x)=-\infty\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.title: Proper Inputs Need Not Give a Proper Infimal Convolution

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Biconjugate Dual of an Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual maximization and closure boundary associated with the infimal-convolution conjugacy identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f,g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions and suppose \(h=f\square g\) is proper. Then
\[
\sup_{y\in\mathbb R^n}\{\langle y,x\rangle-f^*(y)-g^*(y)\}=h^{**}(x)\leq h(x).
\]
Equality at \(x\) holds exactly when \(h(x)=h^{**}(x)\), in particular whenever \(h\) is lower semicontinuous at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing an infimal convolution a second time yields its biconjugate; the dual value equals the original function exactly where no closure gap occurs.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper convex functions on \(\mathbb R^n\).
\(h=f\square g\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_y\{\langle y,x\rangle-f^*(y)-g^*(y)\}=h^{**}(x)\leq h(x)\), with equality exactly where \(h=h^{**}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Biconjugate Dual of an Infimal Convolution

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infimal-Convolution Representation and Its Conjugate Dual
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \[\mathcal H\text{ is a real Hilbert space},\qquad f,g:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty].\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real infimal convolution on a Hilbert space. Exactness, properness, and lower semicontinuity are separate properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The infimal convolution of \(f\) and \(g\) is \[(f\square g)(x):=\inf_{y\in\mathcal H}\{f(y)+g(x-y)\}=\inf_{u+v=x}\{f(u)+g(v)\}.\] Its conjugate-side dual representation is the pointwise sum \[(f\square g)^*(z)=f^*(z)+g^*(z)\] whenever the extended-real expressions are proper; the common dual argument records the multiplier of the coupling equation \(u+v=x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal convolution minimizes the sum of two functions over all decompositions of a point, \(x=u+v\). Conjugation turns this decomposition operation into addition of conjugates at a common dual vector: \((f\square g)^*=f^*+g^*\), subject to the usual properness conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(f\square g)(x)=\inf_{u+v=x}[f(u)+g(v)],\qquad (f\square g)^*=f^*+g^*.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}(f\square g)\supseteq\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g,\] with equality when the infimal convolution is exact at every point of its domain.
special_cases_latex: For sets \(C,D\), \(\delta_C\square\delta_D=\delta_{C+D}\) when every relevant decomposition is attained.
The convolution is exact at \(x\) when some \(y\) attains \((f\square g)(x)=f(y)+g(x-y)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The domain satisfies \(\operatorname{dom}(f\square g)=\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g\).
Infimal convolution is commutative: \(f\square g=g\square f\).
boundary_notes: The infimum need not be attained, even for proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
The infimal convolution of two closed convex functions need not itself be closed without additional conditions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate Duality Induced by a Perturbation Function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \[X=\mathbb R^n,\quad U=\mathbb R^m,\quad F:U\times X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ proper convex},\quad p(u)=\inf_xF(u,x).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional abstract conjugate duality based on a chosen perturbation bifunction. Different perturbations of the same objective can generate different dual problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The abstract conjugate dual of the primal program \[(P)\quad \inf_{x\in X}F(0,x)=p(0)\] is the concave maximization problem \[(D)\quad \sup_{u^*\in U^*}\{-p^*(u^*)\}=\sup_{u^*\in U^*}\inf_{u,x}\{F(u,x)-\langle u^*,u\rangle\}.\] Thus an abstract conjugate-duality pair is the ordered data \((F,0;p,-p^*)\), not merely the unperturbed objective \(F(0,\cdot)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Abstract conjugate duality starts from a convex perturbation bifunction, forms its marginal value function \(p\), and pairs the unperturbed value \(p(0)\) with maximization of \(-p^*\). The perturbation architecture is part of the definition because it determines the dual variables and dual objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(P):\ p(0),\qquad (D):\ \sup_{u^*}-p^*(u^*),\qquad p(u)=\inf_xF(u,x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The dual function can be written \(d(u^*)=\inf_{u,x}[F(u,x)-\langle u^*,u\rangle]\).
special_cases_latex: Choosing an additive linear-composition perturbation recovers Fenchel–Rockafellar duality.
Choosing right-hand-side constraint perturbations recovers the usual Lagrangian dual.
immediate_consequences_latex: The dual optimal value depends only on the closed convex hull of \(p\).
boundary_notes: No topology-free infinite-dimensional version is intended; continuous duals and lower-semicontinuity must then be specified.
The definition does not assert normality, zero gap, or existence of dual optimizers.

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of the perturbation function.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \[F: \mathbb R^m\rightrightarrows\operatorname{Fun}(\mathbb R^n,(-\infty,+\infty]),\qquad \phi(u,x):=(Fu)(x).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rockafellar's finite-dimensional bifunction adjoint. The adjoint reverses the parameter and decision spaces and changes convex minimization into concave maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex bifunction \(F\) from \(\mathbb R^m\) to \(\mathbb R^n\), its adjoint is the concave bifunction \(F^*\) from \(\mathbb R^n\) to \(\mathbb R^m\) defined for every \(x^*\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(u^*\in\mathbb R^m\) by \[\bigl(F^*x^*\bigr)(u^*):=\inf_{u\in\mathbb R^m,\,x\in\mathbb R^n}\{(Fu)(x)-\langle x,x^*\rangle+\langle u,u^*\rangle\}.\] The dual program of the convex program associated with \(F\) maximizes the objective \(F^*0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The adjoint bifunction is obtained by taking a signed full conjugate of the graph function of \(F\). It reverses the roles of parameter and decision spaces: \((F^*x^*)(u^*)\) is the infimum of \((Fu)(x)-\langle x,x^*\rangle+\langle u,u^*\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F^*:x^*\mapsto\left[u^*\mapsto\inf_{u,x}\bigl((Fu)(x)-\langle x,x^*\rangle+\langle u,u^*\rangle\bigr)\right].\]
special_cases_latex: For the indicator bifunction of a linear map \(A\), the construction reduces, up to the stated sign convention, to the ordinary adjoint map \(A^*\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The primal objective is \(F0\), while the dual objective is the concave function \(F^*0\).
boundary_notes: The signs in the definition are convention-dependent and must be kept consistent with the chosen convex and concave conjugates.

\varphi(0)+\varphi^*(\bar y^*)=0,

equivalently when \(\bar y^*\in\partial\varphi(0)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Bifunction Conjugate Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex bifunction produces a primal value at zero perturbation and a conjugate dual value. Weak duality is unconditional, while relative-interior regularity gives equality and a dual maximizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
\varphi(y)=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,y),\qquad p=\varphi(0)=\inf_xF(x,0),
\]
and define
\[
d=\sup_{y^*\in Y^*}-F^*(0,y^*).
\]
Then \(d\le p\). Moreover, \(F^*(0,y^*)=\varphi^*(y^*)\), so \(d=\varphi^{**}(0)\). If \(p\in\mathbb R\) and \(0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{proj}_Y\operatorname{dom}F)\), then \(p=d\), and the supremum is attained.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(F:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\le p\); if \(p\in\mathbb R\) and \(0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{proj}_Y\operatorname{dom}F)\), then \(p=d\) and the dual maximum is attained.

F(x,0)+F^*(0,y^*)\geq0.

(0,y^*)\in\partial F(x,0).

knowledge_statements.title: Bifunction Fenchel-Equality Certificate
Bifunction Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax duality generated by a convex-concave saddle bifunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be convex sets and let \(L:X\times Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex in its first argument and concave in its second. Define
\[
p=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y),\qquad d=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y).
\]
The minimax inequality always gives \(d\le p\). A pair \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is a saddle point precisely when
\[
L(\bar x,y)\le L(\bar x,\bar y)\le L(x,\bar y)
\]
for every \(x\in X\) and \(y\in Y\). Any saddle point yields \(p=d=L(\bar x,\bar y)\), with \(\bar x\) primal optimal and \(\bar y\) dual optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex-concave bifunction defines primal and dual minimax values. Every saddle point certifies equality and attainment of both values.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty convex sets.
\(L\) is convex in its first argument and concave in its second.
\(L\) has no undefined arithmetic at the displayed minimax values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\le p\), and any saddle point \((\bar x,\bar y)\) gives \(p=d=L(\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: Primal minimax and dual maximin values.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(v:Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) by
\[
v(y)=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,y).
\]
Then, for every \(y^*\in Y^*\),
\[
v^*(y^*)=F^*(0,y^*).

Consequently the bifunction dual objective \(-F^*(0,y^*)\) is exactly \(-v^*(y^*)\).

Adjoint Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear composition moves to the dual through the adjoint map. Fenchel conjugates give the dual objective, with strong duality under a relative-interior qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the primal problem
\[
p=\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(f(x)+g(Ax)\bigr),
\]
the adjoint dual problem is
\[
d=\sup_{y^*\in Y^*}\bigl(-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\bigr).
\]
One always has \(d\le p\). If \(p\) is finite and \(0\in\operatorname{ri}(A(\operatorname{dom}f)-\operatorname{dom}g)\), then \(p=d\); moreover, the dual supremum is attained when the common value is finite.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces and \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The adjoint dual is \(\sup_{y^*}\{-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\}\), and its value equals the primal value under the qualification.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel Gap Certificate for the Adjoint Pair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise optimality certificate for the linearly composed Fenchel primal–dual pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in X\) and \(y^*\in Y^*\), set
\[
\Gamma(x,y^*)=f(x)+f^*(-A^*y^*)+g(Ax)+g^*(y^*).
\]
Then \(\Gamma(x,y^*)\geq0\), and
\[
\Gamma(x,y^*)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
-A^*y^*\in\partial f(x)\ \text{ and }\ y^*\in\partial g(Ax).
\]
A zero-gap pair is simultaneously primal optimal and adjoint-dual optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The adjoint primal–dual gap is the sum of two Fenchel–Young gaps and vanishes exactly under the two adjoint-linked subgradient conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional paired real vector spaces.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper convex functions.
\(A:X\to Y\) is linear.

Product-Conjugate Bifunction–Adjoint Identity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encoding a linear composition as an additive perturbation makes the restricted bifunction conjugate exactly equal to the adjoint dual objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F(x,y)=f(x)+g(Ax+y)\),
\[
F^*(x^*,y^*)=f^*(x^*-A^*y^*)+g^*(y^*).
\]
In particular,
\[
-F^*(0,y^*)=-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*),
\]
so the bifunction dual \(\sup_{y^*}-F^*(0,y^*)\) and the adjoint linear-composite dual have exactly the same objective and parameterization.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces and \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, and \(F(x,y)=f(x)+g(Ax+y)\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact identification of linearly coupled bifunction and adjoint dual objectives.
Equivalence of the bifunction and adjoint regularity sets for the additive linear-composite perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x,y)=f(x)+g(Ax+y)\). Then
\[
\operatorname{proj}_Y\operatorname{dom}F
=\operatorname{dom}g-A(\operatorname{dom}f).
\]
Consequently,
\[
0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{proj}_Y\operatorname{dom}F)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0\in\operatorname{ri}(A(\operatorname{dom}f)-\operatorname{dom}g).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the additive perturbation encoding, the bifunction perturbation domain and the adjoint regularity set differ only by reflection, so their relative-interior qualifications are equivalent.
assumptions_latex: \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partial conjugation converts a convex perturbation bifunction into its saddle formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper closed convex bifunction \(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), define the associated saddle bifunction
\[
L_F(x,u^*)=\inf_{u\in U}\{F(x,u)-\langle u^*,u\rangle\}.
\]
For each \(x\), Fenchel biconjugacy of \(F(x,\cdot)\) gives
\[
F(x,0)=\sup_{u^*\in U^*}L_F(x,u^*).
\]
Moreover, for every \(u^*\),
\[
\inf_{x\in X}L_F(x,u^*)=-F^*(0,u^*).
\]
Thus the bifunction minimax pair generated by \(L_F\) is exactly the adjoint pair
\[
\inf_x F(x,0),\qquad \sup_{u^*}\{-F^*(0,u^*)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial conjugation turns a convex perturbation into a saddle bifunction, and its minimax primal-dual pair coincides with the full-conjugate adjoint pair.
assumptions_latex: \(X,U\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper closed convex.
Each slice \(F(x,\cdot)\) used in the identity is proper.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Process Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex process is dualized by polarizing its conic graph; the resulting adjoint process is characterized by a pairing inequality on every graph element.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The adjoint convex process \(T^*:Y^*\rightrightarrows X^*\) is defined by
\[
x^*\in T^*(y^*)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\langle x^*,x\rangle\le \langle y^*,y\rangle
\quad\text{for every }(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}T.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
(x^*,-y^*)\in(\operatorname{gph}T)^\circ,
\]
where the polar cone convention is \(C^\circ=\{z^*: \langle z^*,z\rangle\le0\text{ for all }z\in C\}\). This polar relation converts inclusions involving \(T\) into dual inequalities involving \(T^*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every closed proper convex function is reconstructed as the supremum of all continuous affine minorants supplied by epigraph separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a finite-dimensional space, then \[f(x)=\sup\{\langle x^*,x\rangle-\beta:\langle x^*,z\rangle-\beta\le f(z)\ \forall z\in X\}.\] Thus \(f\) is the pointwise supremum of all its continuous affine minorants.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Separation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point strictly below a closed convex epigraph can be separated from it by the graph of an affine minorant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exist \(x^*\in X^*\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\) such that
\[
r_0<\langle x^*,x_0\rangle-\beta
\quad\text{and}\quad
\langle x^*,x\rangle-\beta\le t
\quad\text{for every }(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f.
\]
Hence the graph of the affine function \(x\mapsto\langle x^*,x\rangle-\beta\) strictly separates the point from the epigraph and supplies a global affine minorant of \(f\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\((x_0,r_0)\notin\operatorname{epi}f\) with \(r_0<f(x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonvertical affine hyperplane strictly separates \((x_0,r_0)\) from \(\operatorname{epi}f\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: What continuous affine minorants recover when a proper convex epigraph is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f\) is proper and convex, then
\[
\sup\{a:a\text{ is continuous affine and }a\le f\}=f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}f\le f.
\]
Thus, when \(f\ne\operatorname{cl}f\), separation by continuous affine minorants recovers the lower-semicontinuous convex closure rather than the omitted boundary values of \(f\).

\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex.

f(x)=\sup\{a(x):a:X\to\mathbb R\text{ is continuous affine and }a\le f\}

knowledge_statements.title: Nonvertical Separation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A product-space hyperplane is nonvertical exactly when its height coefficient is nonzero; it can then be normalized as an affine graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Write
\[
H=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb R:\langle x^*,x\rangle+\alpha t=\beta\},
\]
with \((x^*,\alpha)\ne(0,0)\). The hyperplane is nonvertical precisely when \(\alpha\ne0\). In that case division by \(-\alpha\) yields
\[
H=\{(x,t):t=\langle u^*,x\rangle+b\},
\qquad
u^*=-x^*/\alpha,\quad b=\beta/\alpha,
\]
so \(H\) is the graph of an affine functional. If \(\alpha=0\), membership is independent of \(t\), and \(H\) is vertical.

\(H\subset X\times\mathbb R\) is an affine hyperplane.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The min-common problem associated with \(M\) is \[w^*:=\inf\{w:(0,w)\in M\}.\] For each \(\mu\in\mathbb R^n\), the highest crossing level of a nonvertical hyperplane with normal \((\mu,1)\) whose upper halfspace contains \(M\) is \[q(\mu):=\inf_{(u,w)\in M}\{w+\langle\mu,u\rangle\}.\] The max-crossing problem is \[q^*:=\sup_{\mu\in\mathbb R^n}q(\mu).\] The ordered pair of these optimization problems is the min-common/max-crossing dual pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The min-common problem seeks the lowest common point of the set \(M\) and the vertical axis. The max-crossing problem seeks the highest vertical-axis crossing among nonvertical hyperplanes whose upper halfspaces contain \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[w^*=\inf_{(0,w)\in M}w,qquad q^*=\sup_{\mu\in\mathbb R^n}\inf_{(u,w)\in M}[w+\langle\mu,u\rangle].\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For fixed \(\mu\), admissible hyperplanes are \(H_{\mu,\xi}=\{(u,w):w+\langle\mu,u\rangle=\xi\}\) with \(\xi\leq q(\mu)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(M=\operatorname{epi}p\), the min-common value is \(p(0)\) and \(q(\mu)=-p^*(-\mu)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The construction gives \(q^*\leq w^*\).
Replacing \(M\) by \(M+\{(0,t):t\geq0\}\) leaves both values unchanged.
boundary_notes: If \(M\cap\ell=\varnothing\), then \(w^*=+\infty\).
If the upward extension contains a vertical line, the max-crossing problem may have value \(-\infty\).

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Point Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of a finite pointwise maximum is the intersection of the individual epigraphs. Thus the minimax value is the infimum height of their common points, and attained solutions correspond exactly to lowest common points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\),
\[
\operatorname{epi}F=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{epi}f_i.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\inf_{x\in X}\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)
=
\inf\{t\in\mathbb R:\exists x\in X\text{ with }(x,t)\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{epi}f_i\}.
\]
If the infimum is attained at \(\bar x\), then \((\bar x,F(\bar x))\) is a common epigraph point of minimum height; conversely, the first coordinate of every minimum-height common epigraph point minimizes \(F\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper convex functions.
\(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}f_i\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The infimum of the pointwise maximum equals the infimum height of the common epigraph, and attained minimizers correspond to its lowest points.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph-intersection representation for finite minimax common-point geometry.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Helly Certificate for Fixed-Height Common Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional infeasibility certificate for a horizontal slice of the common epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d=\dim X\) and \(L_i(t)=\{x\in X:f_i(x)\le t\}\). Then
\[
\{x:(x,t)\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{epi}f_i\}=\bigcap_{i=1}^mL_i(t).
\]
Moreover, this intersection is empty if and only if some \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) with \(|I|\le d+1\) satisfies
\[
\bigcap_{i\in I}L_i(t)=\varnothing.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a fixed height, common epigraph points form the intersection of the corresponding convex sublevel sets. Helly's theorem gives an infeasible subfamily of at most dimension plus one sets.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space with \(d=\dim X\).
\(f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are convex.
\(m\ge1\) and \(t\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixed-height common-point infeasibility is witnessed by at most \(d+1\) functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Helly Certificate for Fixed-Height Common Points
Crossing-Hyperplane Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A crossing affine hyperplane has, at every common-domain point, a height lying between the smallest and largest values of the function family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The affine hyperplane
\[
H_a=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb R:t=a(x)\}
\]
is crossing for the family \((f_i)_{i=1}^m\) when
\[
\min_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\le a(x)\le\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)
\quad\text{for every }x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}f_i.
\]
Equivalently, at each common-domain point, \(H_a\) meets the vertical interval whose endpoints are the smallest and largest function values. The quantifier and domain convention are part of this definition.
assumptions_latex: \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) are given functions.
\(a(x)=\langle x^*,x\rangle+\beta\) is affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed pointwise inequalities are the crossing predicate for the affine hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Candidate pointwise crossing predicate; the intended literature convention requires confirmation.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \[M\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R,\qquad \mu\in\mathbb R^n,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional hyperplane geometry with a distinguished vertical axis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The crossing hyperplane with slope parameter \(\mu\) and crossing level \(\xi\) is \[H_{\mu,\xi}:=\{(u,w):w+\langle\mu,u\rangle=\xi\}.\] It crosses the vertical axis at \((0,\xi)\). It is an upper supporting crossing hyperplane for \(M\) when \[w+\langle\mu,u\rangle\geq\xi\qquad\forall(u,w)\in M.\] For fixed \(\mu\), its maximal admissible crossing level is \[q_M(\mu):=\inf_{(u,w)\in M}\{w+\langle\mu,u\rangle\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A crossing hyperplane is normalized so that the coefficient of the height variable is one. Its scalar constant is exactly its vertical-axis crossing level. Requiring the set \(M\) to lie in the upper halfspace bounds that level above by \(q_M(\mu)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[H_{\mu,\xi}\text{ supports }M\text{ from below}\iff \xi\leq q_M(\mu).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[q_M(\mu)=-\sigma_M(-\mu,-1),\] whenever the extended support-function convention is used.
special_cases_latex: For \(M=\operatorname{epi}p\), \(q_M(\mu)=\inf_u[p(u)+\langle\mu,u\rangle]\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The function \(q_M\) is concave because it is a pointwise infimum of affine functions of \(\mu\).
boundary_notes: Vertical hyperplanes cannot be written in the normalized form \(H_{\mu,\xi}\).
The infimum defining \(q_M(\mu)\) need not be attained, so the extremal hyperplane need not touch \(M\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar Set and Polar Gauge Correspondence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \[E\text{ is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space},\qquad C\subseteq E\text{ is nonempty, convex, and }0\in C.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polarity for convex sets containing the origin and their Minkowski gauges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The gauge and polar set of \(C\) are \[\gamma_C(x):=\inf\{\lambda\geq0:x\in\lambda C\},\qquad C^\circ:=\{y\in E:\langle y,x\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\}.\] For any gauge \(\kappa\), its polar gauge is \[\kappa^\circ(y):=\sup_{x\neq0}\frac{\langle y,x\rangle}{\kappa(x)}=\sup\{\langle y,x\rangle:\kappa(x)\leq1\}.\] The polar-gauge correspondence is \[(\gamma_C)^\circ=\gamma_{C^\circ},\qquad \kappa^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\kappa.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gauge measures the smallest nonnegative scaling of \(C\) containing a point. The polar set consists of linear functionals bounded by one on \(C\). Taking the polar gauge exchanges \(C\) with \(C^\circ\), and applying polarity twice closes the original gauge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(\gamma_C)^\circ=\gamma_{C^\circ},\qquad \kappa^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\kappa.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\kappa^\circ(y)=\inf\{\mu\geq0:\langle y,x\rangle\leq\mu\kappa(x)\ \forall x\}.\]
special_cases_latex [
special_cases_latex: For a norm, the polar gauge is its dual norm.
For a closed convex set \(C\) containing \(0\), the polar gauge of \(\gamma_C\) equals the support function \(\sigma_C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The generalized Hölder inequality \(\langle y,x\rangle\leq\kappa(x)\kappa^\circ(y)\) holds on the effective domains.
Closed gauges occur in symmetric polar pairs.
boundary_notes: If \(C\) is not absorbing, \(\gamma_C\) may take the value \(+\infty\).
If \(C\) is not closed, bisection by polarity returns its closed convex hull containing the origin.

knowledge_statements.title: General Bipolar Closure Formula
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bipolar is the closed convex hull obtained after adjoining the origin, and polarity reverses inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(S\subset X\), with \(S^\circ=\{y\in X^*:\langle y,x\rangle\le1\ \forall x\in S\}\), one has \[S^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S\cup\{0\}).\] Moreover, polarity reverses inclusion: \(S\subset T\Rightarrow T^\circ\subset S^\circ\). Consequently, \(S^{\circ\circ}=S\) exactly when \(S\) is closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional paired real vector space.
\(S,T\subset X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S\cup\{0\}),\qquad S\subset T\Rightarrow T^\circ\subset S^\circ.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp set-bipolar formula without prior closedness, convexity, or origin-containment assumptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Polar Dual Models
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set containing the origin is recovered from its polar, whose points pair with every primal point by at most one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The polar of \(C\) is
\[
C^\circ=\{y\in X^*: \langle y,x\rangle\le1\text{ for every }x\in C\}
      =\{y\in X^*: \sigma_C(y)\le1\}.
\]
Its bipolar satisfies
\[
C^{\circ\circ}=C.
\]
Accordingly, either member of the pair \((C,C^\circ)\) determines the other, and feasibility in one model is expressed by a uniform unit upper bound on pairings with the other model.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional paired real vector space.
\(C\subset X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The polar model is involutive: \(C^{\circ\circ}=C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-polar duality with unit-level normalization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Order and Set-Operation Calculus for Polars
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contravariant calculus of unit-normalized set polarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For subsets \(A,B\subset X\),
\[
A\subseteq B\implies B^\circ\subseteq A^\circ,
\qquad
(\lambda A)^\circ=\lambda^{-1}A^\circ\quad(\lambda>0).
\]
For every family \((A_j)_{j\in J}\),
\[
\left(\operatorname{conv}\bigcup_{j\in J}A_j\right)^\circ
=
\bigcap_{j\in J}A_j^\circ.
\]
If \(A\) and \(B\) are closed and convex and contain \(0\), then
\[
(A\cap B)^\circ=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(A^\circ\cup B^\circ).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity reverses inclusion and positive scaling, sends convex hulls of unions to intersections, and sends intersections of closed convex origin-containing sets to closed convex hulls of their polars.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional.
All polars use the unit upper-pairing convention.
The intersection identity assumes that \(A\) and \(B\) are closed, convex, and contain \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polarity obeys the stated contravariant order, scaling, hull, and intersection identities.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar Dual of a Gauge-Constrained Model
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \[X,Y\text{ are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces},\quad A:X\to Y\text{ linear},\quad b\in Y,\quad \sigma\geq0,\] \[\kappa:X\to[0,+\infty],\quad \rho:Y\to[0,+\infty]\text{ are closed gauges}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional gauge optimization model with a residual gauge constraint. The normalization of the polar dual uses a unit lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the gauge primal model \[(P)\quad \inf_{x\in X}\{\kappa(x):\rho(b-Ax)\leq\sigma\},\] define the polar dual model by \[(D_p)\quad \inf_{y\in Y}\{\kappa^\circ(A^*y):\langle b,y\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(y)\geq1\}.\] Here \(\kappa^\circ\) and \(\rho^\circ\) are the polar gauges. The constraint is positively homogeneous in \(y\), so every feasible nonzero ray is represented by its normalization at level one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polar dual model replaces the primal gauge by its polar evaluated at the adjoint image of a dual vector. The residual constraint becomes the homogeneous normalization \(\langle b,y\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(y)\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{PolarDual}(P):\quad \min_y\ \kappa^\circ(A^*y)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \langle b,y\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(y)\geq1.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: When the denominator is positive, the dual value equals \(\inf_y\kappa^\circ(A^*y)/(\langle b,y\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(y))\).
special_cases_latex: For \(sigma=0\), the normalization reduces to \(langle b,yranglegeq1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Positive homogeneity permits rescaling any \(y\) with positive denominator to satisfy the constraint at equality.
boundary_notes: Feasibility requires some \(y\) with \(\langle b,y\rangle>\sigma\rho^\circ(y)\).
The precise reciprocal value relation and attainment conditions require a polar-duality theorem and are not included in this definition.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Qualified Model Without Primal Attainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even a closed convex qualified model can lack a primal minimizer when the gauge is noncoercive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(X=\mathbb R^2\), let \(\kappa(s,t)=\max\{s,0\}\) and \(C=\{(s,t):s\ge1+e^{-t}\}\). Then \(\kappa\) is a proper closed gauge, \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}\kappa)\cap\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing\). Nevertheless, \(v_p=1\) and no point of \(C\) attains this value.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Gauge Duality Under Relative-Interior Qualification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relative-interior qualification and a positive finite primal value give reciprocal gauge-dual values and attainment of the gauge dual, but not necessarily of the primal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite-dimensional, let \(\kappa:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be a proper closed gauge, and let \(C\subset X\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Define \(C'=\{y\in X^*:\langle y,x\rangle\ge1\ \forall x\in C\}\), \(v_p=\inf_{x\in C}\kappa(x)\), and \(v_d=\inf_{y\in C'}\kappa^\circ(y)\). If \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}\kappa)\cap\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing\) and \(0<v_p<+\infty\), then the gauge dual attains its minimum and \(v_pv_d=1\). These assumptions alone do not assert primal attainment.

\(\kappa\) is a proper closed gauge.
\(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}\kappa)\cap\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume \(0<v_p,v_d<+\infty\) and \(v_pv_d=1\). For a feasible pair \((x,y)\in C\times C'\), joint primal-dual optimality is equivalent to
\[
\kappa(x)\kappa^\circ(y)=1.
\]
In this case
\[
1\le\langle y,x\rangle\le\kappa(x)\kappa^\circ(y)=1,
\]
so \(\langle y,x\rangle=1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Pair Gauge Optimality Certificate
Gauge Dual Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued gauge and polar-gauge models generated by a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\) be closed and convex with \(0\in C\). Its gauge is
\[
\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t\geq 0:x\in tC\},
\]
where the infimum of the empty set is \(+\infty\). The polar gauge is
\[
\gamma_C^\circ(y)=\sup\{\langle y,x\rangle:\gamma_C(x)\leq1\}.
\]
Since the unit sublevel set of \(\gamma_C\) is \(C\), one has \(\gamma_C^\circ=\sigma_C\); equivalently, the polar gauge is the support function of the primal gauge unit set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex set containing zero defines a gauge by radial scaling; its polar gauge is the support function of the unit set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C^\circ(y)=\sigma_C(y)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle\).

Then \[\gamma_C^*=\delta_{C^\circ},\qquad \sigma_C^*=\delta_C.\] Together with \(\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ}\) and \(\sigma_C=\gamma_{C^\circ}\), these identities recover the polar and primal sets from the corresponding functional representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Support–Gauge Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex set containing zero, its gauge is the support function of its polar, and its support function is the gauge of its polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
With
\[
\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{\lambda\ge0:x\in\lambda C\}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\sigma_C(y)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle,
\]
one has
\[
\gamma_C(x)=\sigma_{C^\circ}(x)
\quad\text{for every }x\in X,
\qquad
\sigma_C(y)=\gamma_{C^\circ}(y)
\quad\text{for every }y\in X^*.
\]
Thus polarity exchanges the unit sublevel set of a gauge with the support representation of that gauge.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional paired real vector space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finiteness Boundaries for Support and Gauge
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric conditions controlling everywhere finiteness of the corresponding functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In finite dimension,
\[
\gamma_C(x)<+\infty\ \text{for every }x\in X
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
C\text{ is absorbing}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0\in\operatorname{int}C,
\]
whereas
\[
\sigma_C(y)<+\infty\ \text{for every }y\in X^*
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
C\text{ is bounded}.
\]
The support–gauge identities remain valid as extended-real identities when either finiteness condition fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gauge is finite everywhere exactly when the set absorbs the space, while the support function is finite everywhere exactly when the set is bounded; neither condition is needed for the extended-real correspondence.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional.
\(C\subset X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Everywhere finiteness of \(\gamma_C\) is equivalent to absorption, and everywhere finiteness of \(\sigma_C\) is equivalent to boundedness.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\delta_C\) be the indicator of \(C\). Then
\[
\delta_C^*=\sigma_C,
\qquad
\sigma_C^*=\delta_C,
\qquad
\gamma_C^*=\delta_{C^\circ}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
C^\circ=\{y\in X^*:\langle y,x\rangle\le\gamma_C(x)\text{ for every }x\in X\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function is conjugate to the set indicator, and the gauge is conjugate to the indicator of the polar; the polar is equivalently the set of functionals dominated by the gauge.

\(C\subset X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_C^*=\sigma_C\), \(\sigma_C^*=\delta_C\), and \(\gamma_C^*=\delta_{C^\circ}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauge as the Support Function of the Polar Set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, and let \(C\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex set containing \(0\). Extended-real values are allowed, with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex sets containing the origin; the gauge may be extended-valued when the set is not absorbing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The gauge and polar of \(C\) are \[\gamma_C(x):=\inf\{t\geq 0:x\in tC\},\qquad C^\circ:=\{y\in E:\langle y,z\rangle\leq 1\ \forall z\in C\}.\] The support–gauge correspondence is \[\gamma_C(x)=\sigma_{C^\circ}(x):=\sup_{y\in C^\circ}\langle x,y\rangle\qquad(\forall x\in E).\] Equivalently, \(\gamma_C^*=\delta_{C^\circ}\), where \(\delta_{C^\circ}\) is the indicator of \(C^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex set containing the origin, its gauge is the infimum of nonnegative dilations needed to contain a point, and its polar consists of vectors whose pairing with every point of the set is at most one. The gauge at every point equals the support function of the polar at that point. Equivalently, the convex conjugate of the gauge is the indicator function of the polar.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
\(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, with \(0\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ}\) on \(E\), equivalently \(\gamma_C^*=\delta_{C^\circ}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C=\{x\in E:\gamma_C(x)\leq 1\}\).
\(C^\circ=\{y\in E:\sigma_C(y)\leq 1\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is the closed unit ball of a norm \(\|\cdot\|\), then \(\gamma_C(x)=\|x\|\) and \(\sigma_{C^\circ}(x)=\|x\|\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\gamma_C\) is convex and positively homogeneous.
The polar determines \(C\) through \(C=C^{\circ\circ}\) under the stated hypotheses.
boundary_notes: If \(C\) is not closed and convex, the bipolar operation returns \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\})\), so the displayed reconstruction need not recover the original set.
If \(C\) is not absorbing, \(\gamma_C(x)=+\infty\) may occur.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a closed convex cone, \(K^*:=\{y:\langle y,s\rangle\geq0\ \forall s\in K\}\), \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) linear, and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic linear optimization in inequality form; this definition constructs the dual but does not assert strong duality or attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The conic primal problem and its dual are the ordered pair \[(P)\quad p^*:=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{c^Tx:Ax-b\in K\},\] \[(D)\quad d^*:=\sup_{y\in\mathbb R^m}\{b^Ty:A^Ty=c,\ y\in K^*\}.\] Conic duality is the correspondence that replaces the primal cone order by the dual-cone multiplier condition and imposes \(A^Ty=c\), so every dual-feasible \(y\) supplies the lower bound \(b^Ty\) for the minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a linear objective and a constraint that the slack belongs to a closed convex cone, the conic dual maximizes the pairing with the right-hand side over multipliers in the dual cone whose adjoint image equals the primal objective vector. The pair is defined independently of whether either feasible set is nonempty, either value is finite, or either optimum is attained.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is a closed convex cone.
\(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, with data \(b\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((P),(D)\) form the conic primal–dual pair with feasible sets \(\{x:Ax-b\in K\}\) and \(\{y\in K^*:A^Ty=c\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using \(u\succeq_K v\iff u-v\in K\), the primal constraint is \(Ax\succeq_K b\).
The dual objective is the best bound obtainable by scalarizing \(Ax\succeq_K b\) with an order-preserving linear functional.
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R_+^m\), one obtains the standard inequality-form linear-programming dual.
For a self-dual cone \(K=K^*\), primal slacks and dual multipliers belong to the same cone.
immediate_consequences_latex: For every feasible pair \((x,y)\), \(c^Tx-b^Ty=\langle y,Ax-b\rangle\geq0\).
Dualizing the geometric conic form again recovers an equivalent primal problem when \(K=K^{**}\).
boundary_notes: Strong duality and attainment require additional hypotheses such as appropriate strict feasibility.
Sign conventions change if the primal cone inequality or optimization orientation is reversed.
