knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-Order Coupling and the Bilinear Remainder
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local residual geometry when both the constraint operator and right-hand-side data vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(r(x;E,d)=(A+E)x-(b+d)\). For a decision displacement \(h\),
\[r(x+h;E,d)-r(x;0,0)=Ah+Ex-d+Eh.\]
Thus the operator and decision perturbations have the bilinear remainder \(Eh\). Moreover,
\[\|Ex-d\|\leq \|E\|\,\|x\|+\|d\|.\]
Consequently, small \((E,d)\) gives a uniform small residual displacement on bounded decision sets, but operator-norm smallness alone gives no uniform bound over an unbounded decision set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simultaneous operator and data perturbations have a bilinear operator–decision interaction. Uniform residual control requires bounded decisions or another bound on their size.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces.
\(A,E\in\mathcal L(X,Y)\), \(b,d\in Y\), and the operator norm is subordinate to the chosen norms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exact residual expansion contains the coupling term \(Eh\), and uniform control by \(\|E\|\) requires control of decision magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Coupling and the Bilinear Remainder
Nominal Equivalence Does Not Preserve Calmness Moduli
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two parameterizations can define the same nominal problem yet have different exact local sensitivity moduli.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[P_1(u):\ \min_x |x|\ \text{ subject to }x=u,\qquad P_2(w):\ \min_x |x|\ \text{ subject to }x=w^2.\]
At parameter zero the problems have the same objective, feasible set \(\{0\}\), optimizer, and value. Their value functions are \(v_1(u)=|u|\) and \(v_2(w)=w^2\). Their exact calmness moduli at zero, defined by the corresponding local limsup ratios, are respectively \(1\) and \(0\).
assumptions_latex: Parameters and decisions are real scalars with the absolute-value norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nominal feasible-set and objective equivalence does not determine perturbational calmness.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit boundary between nominal equivalence and equivalence of perturbation geometry.

notation.meaning: Two parameterized representations of the same nominal problem

knowledge_statements.title: Calmness Transfer Under Bi-Lipschitz Reparameterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value-preserving local bi-Lipschitz coordinate change transfers calmness in both directions, with constants scaled by coordinate distortion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v_1,v_2\) be finite-valued near their reference parameters. Suppose neighborhoods of \(0\) are related by a bijection \(\phi\) satisfying
\[\phi(0)=0,\quad v_2(\phi(u))=v_1(u),\quad \|\phi(u)\|\leq L\|u\|,\quad \|\phi^{-1}(w)\|\leq M\|w\|.\]
If \(|v_1(u)-v_1(0)|\leq\kappa_1\|u\|\) locally, then \(|v_2(w)-v_2(0)|\leq M\kappa_1\|w\|\) locally. Conversely, a calmness bound \(\kappa_2\) for \(v_2\) yields the bound \(L\kappa_2\) for \(v_1\).
assumptions_latex: The value functions are finite-valued near zero.
The displayed value-preserving bijection and local forward and inverse Lipschitz bounds hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local calmness transfers bidirectionally with multiplicative factors \(M\) and \(L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient condition for transferring local value sensitivity between representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Sensitivity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent nominal constraints can induce differently scaled perturbation sensitivities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(f(x)=(x-1)^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). The nominal constraints \(x\leq0\) and \(\alpha x\leq0\), with \(\alpha>0\), describe the same feasible set. Perturbing their right-hand sides gives
\[
v_1(u):=\inf_{x\leq u}f(x),\qquad v_\alpha(u):=\inf_{\alpha x\leq u}f(x)=v_1(u/\alpha).
\]
Near \(u=0\), one has \(v_1'(0)=-2\) and \(v_\alpha'(0)=-2/\alpha\). Thus nominal equivalence does not make sensitivity representation-invariant; the boundary is the choice of perturbation coordinates and scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling an equivalent constraint rescales its right-hand-side sensitivity, so nominal equivalence alone does not ensure representation-invariant multipliers or derivatives.
assumptions_latex: Sensitivity is taken with respect to the displayed right-hand-side coordinate \(u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_\alpha(u)=v_1(u/\alpha)\) and \(v_\alpha'(0)=v_1'(0)/\alpha=-2/\alpha\).

notation.meaning: value under the unscaled constraint representation
value under the scaled constraint representation

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v_1:U_1\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(v_2:U_2\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), and suppose neighborhoods of \(0\) are related by a bijection \(\phi\) with \(\phi(0)=0\),
\[v_2(\phi(u))=v_1(u),\qquad \|\phi(u)\|\leq L\|u\|,\qquad \|\phi^{-1}(w)\|\leq M\|w\|.\]
Then calmness of \(v_1\) at \(0\) with modulus \(\kappa_1\) implies calmness of \(v_2\) with modulus at most \(M\kappa_1\), and calmness of \(v_2\) with modulus \(\kappa_2\) implies calmness of \(v_1\) with modulus at most \(L\kappa_2\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local calmness is invariant up to the multiplicative distortions \(L\) and \(M\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(Y=\mathbb{R}^m\), \(U\) be a parameter space, \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), and \(G:X\times U\to Y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued perturbations in which both an admissible decision set and a constraint cone depend on the same parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set-cone perturbation coupling consists of mappings
\[
C:U\rightrightarrows X,
\qquad
K:U\rightrightarrows Y,
\]
such that each \(K(u)\) is a cone, together with nominal objects \(C(0)=C_0\) and \(K(0)=K_0\). The perturbed feasible set and optimal value are
\[
\mathcal{F}(u):=\{x\in C(u):G(x,u)\in-K(u)\},
\qquad
p(u):=\inf_{x\in\mathcal{F}(u)}f(x).
\]
The equivalent extended-real representation is
\[
F(x,u)=f(x)+\delta_{C(u)}(x)+\delta_{-K(u)}(G(x,u)),
\qquad p(u)=\inf_xF(x,u).
\]
The coupling is genuine when the parameter cannot be decomposed as \(u=(u_C,u_K)\) so that \(C\) depends only on \(u_C\) and \(K\) only on \(u_K\). The polar multiplier cone at parameter \(u\) is
\[
K(u)^*:=\{y\in Y:\langle y,k\rangle\ge0\ \text{for every }k\in K(u)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-cone perturbation uses one parameter to vary both the admissible decision set and the cone that orders the constraint residual. Feasible decisions belong to the varying set and have residual in the negative varying cone. Indicator functions combine these requirements into one extended-real objective. The dual multiplier domain changes with the polar of the perturbed cone.
assumptions_latex: \(C(u)\subseteq X\) for every \(u\in U\).
\(K(u)\subseteq Y\) is a cone for every \(u\in U\).
The nominal objects satisfy \(C(0)=C_0\) and \(K(0)=K_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p(u)=\inf_{x\in X}\bigl[f(x)+\delta_{C(u)}(x)+\delta_{-K(u)}(G(x,u))\bigr].\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in\mathcal F(u)\) if and only if \(x\in C(u)\) and \(-G(x,u)\in K(u)\).
When \(K(u)\) is closed and convex, the compatible multiplier domain is its polar cone \(K(u)^*\).
special_cases_latex: Fixed-cone set perturbation: \(K(u)\equiv K_0\).
Fixed-set cone perturbation: \(C(u)\equiv C_0\).
Ordinary scalar inequalities arise from \(Y=\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(K(u)=\mathbb{R}_+^m\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\mathcal F(u)=\varnothing\), then \(p(u)=+\infty\).
Variation of \(K(u)\) changes both primal feasibility and the admissible dual multiplier cone.
boundary_notes: Closedness, convexity, and graphical continuity of the set-valued maps are not part of the bare definition.
No inspected source among the supplied hints directly supported this exact simultaneous set-and-cone formulation.

notation.meaning: The positive polar cone under the stated sign convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled feasible-set and ordering-cone perturbation
Value Monotonicity and Hausdorff Stability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shrinking a feasible set cannot improve a minimization value, and a Lipschitz objective makes the value Lipschitz in Hausdorff distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v(C)=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\). If \(C_1\subseteq C_2\), then \(v(C_1)\geq v(C_2)\). If \(C_1,C_2\) are nonempty compact sets and \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on a set containing them, then
\[|v(C_1)-v(C_2)|\leq Ld_H(C_1,C_2).\]
Consequently, Hausdorff convergence of such feasible sets implies convergence of their optimal values.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is real-valued on the sets under comparison.
For the metric estimate, \(C_1,C_2\) are nonempty compact sets and \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on a common containing set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible-set inclusion reverses value order, and compact Hausdorff perturbations change the value by at most \(Ld_H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order and metric sensitivity of a fixed objective under feasible-set variation.

notation.meaning: Infimum of the fixed objective over C

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Set Perturbations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible-set perturbation replaces the nominal constraint set by a parameterized family; equivalently, it adds each set's indicator to a fixed convex objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(u\in U\), let \(C_u\) be the perturbed feasible set, with nominal set \(C_0\). Define
\[v(u)=\inf_{x\in C_u}f(x)=\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(f(x)+\iota_{C_u}(x)\bigr),\]
where \(\iota_{C_u}(x)=0\) for \(x\in C_u\), \(\iota_{C_u}(x)=+\infty\) otherwise, and \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). Because \(f\) and every \(C_u\) are convex, each extended-real objective \(f+\iota_{C_u}\) is convex.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and \(U\) is a parameter set containing \(0\).
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and each \(C_u\subseteq X\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible-set perturbation is represented by the extended-real objectives \(f+\iota_{C_u}\) and their infima.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued perturbations of feasibility with a fixed convex objective.

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Convex Sets p. 49

knowledge_statements.title: Cone Inclusion Reverses Dual Multipliers
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enlarging an ordering cone relaxes primal conic feasibility but restricts the dual multiplier cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For closed convex cones \(K_1,K_2\subseteq Y\),
\[K_1\subseteq K_2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad K_2^*\subseteq K_1^*.\]
Also \(-K_1\subseteq-K_2\). Thus replacing \(K_1\) by the larger cone \(K_2\) weakens the primal constraint \(G(x)\in-K_i\) while shrinking the admissible dual-multiplier cone.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
\(K_1,K_2\subseteq Y\) are closed convex cones, with duals defined by the nonnegative pairing convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal cone inclusion and dual-cone inclusion run in opposite directions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal and multiplier effects of enlarging an ordering cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordering-Cone Perturbations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perturbing a pointed ordering cone changes the primal partial order and feasible inequalities together with the corresponding dual multiplier cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(u\in U\), an ordering-cone perturbation replaces \(K_0\) by \(K_u\). The induced partial order and dual cone are
\[y_1\preceq_{K_u}y_2\iff y_2-y_1\in K_u,\qquad K_u^*=\{z\in Y:\langle z,k\rangle\geq 0\ \text{for every }k\in K_u\}.\]
Accordingly, a constraint \(G(x)\in-K_u\) and its admissible dual multipliers \(z\in K_u^*\) vary with the same cone. Pointedness ensures that \(\preceq_{K_u}\) is antisymmetric and hence a partial order.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and \(U\) is a parameter set containing \(0\).
Each \(K_u\subseteq Y\) is a closed, convex, pointed cone, with nominal cone \(K_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Changing the ordering cone changes the induced partial order, conic feasibility condition, and dual multiplier cone simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbation of a pointed cone defining conic feasibility, order, and dual multipliers.

notation.meaning: Partial order induced by the pointed cone

knowledge_statements.title: Set–Cone Interaction Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A joint set-cone perturbation intersects a moving closed convex set with the inverse image of a moving cone, yielding feasible, positive-gap infeasible, or zero-gap infeasible regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(u\in U\), define
\[F(u)=C_u\cap G^{-1}(-K_u)=\{x\in C_u:G(x)\in-K_u\}.\]
Because \(G\) is affine and continuous, both \(C_u\) and \(G^{-1}(-K_u)\) are closed and convex. The interaction regime is feasible when \(F(u)\neq\varnothing\), positive-gap infeasible when \(F(u)=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(C_u,G^{-1}(-K_u))>0\), and zero-gap infeasible when \(F(u)=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(C_u,G^{-1}(-K_u))=0\).
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces and \(U\) is a parameter set containing \(0\).
For every \(u\in U\), \(C_u\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(K_u\subseteq Y\) is a closed convex cone.
\(G:X\to Y\) is affine and continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The perturbed feasible geometry is determined jointly by the moving set \(C_u\) and the inverse image \(G^{-1}(-K_u)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint movement of an explicit closed convex set and a conic constraint under a fixed affine map.

knowledge_statements.title: Disjoint Closed Convex Sets with Zero Distance
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exponential epigraph and the horizontal axis are disjoint closed convex sets with zero separation distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In \(\mathbb R^2\), let
\[A=\{(s,t):t\geq e^s\},\qquad B=\{(s,0):s\in\mathbb R\}.\]
Both sets are nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(A\cap B=\varnothing\). Nevertheless,
\[\operatorname{dist}(A,B)=0,\]
since the distance from \((s,e^s)\in A\) to \((s,0)\in B\) tends to zero as \(s\to-\infty\).
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb R^2\) carries its Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Disjointness of closed convex sets does not imply positive distance or a robust infeasibility margin.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete zero-gap infeasibility in finite-dimensional convex geometry.

notation.meaning: The two disjoint closed convex sets

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Stability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive distance makes infeasibility robust under sufficiently small Hausdorff perturbations. Zero-distance infeasibility has no such margin, while failure of relative-interior overlap signals loss of a qualification but does not alone prove instability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(A\cap B=\varnothing\) and \(\delta=\operatorname{dist}(A,B)>0\), strict separation provides a positive-gap infeasibility certificate. Moreover, for nonempty closed sets \(A',B'\) with finite Hausdorff distances satisfying
\[d_H(A,A')+d_H(B,B')<\delta,\]
one has \(\operatorname{dist}(A',B')>0\), so infeasibility persists. If \(A\cap B=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(A,B)=0\), no positive distance margin is available. If \(A\cap B\neq\varnothing\) but \(\operatorname{ri}A\cap\operatorname{ri}B=\varnothing\), the standard relative-interior qualification fails; this failure alone does not determine stability without a specified perturbation model and metric.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
\(A,B\subseteq X\) are nonempty closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive set distance yields a quantitatively robust infeasibility boundary, whereas zero distance yields no positive separation margin; relative-interior intersection is a qualification condition but not by itself an ambient perturbation radius.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional geometric boundaries for convex intersection qualifications and distance-based infeasibility certificates.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(U=\mathbb{R}^r\), and \(F:X\times U\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real value functions obtained by minimizing over decisions or latent variables, including constraint right-hand-side values as a principal specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The value, marginal, perturbation, or primal function associated with \(F\) is the partial infimum
\[
p:U\to\overline{\mathbb{R}},
\qquad
p(u):=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u).
\]
Its effective domain and exact argmin fiber are
\[
\operatorname{dom}p=\{u:p(u)<+\infty\},
\qquad
M(u)=\{x:F(x,u)=p(u)\}.
\]
For a constrained family with \(C(u)=\{x\in X:g(x)\le u,\ Ax+b=t\}\), the two-parameter value function is
\[
v(u,t)=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ g(x)\le u,\ Ax+b=t\},
\]
with the convention \(v(u,t)=+\infty\) when the feasible set is empty. If \(F\) is jointly convex, then \(p\) is convex. In the inequality-coordinate specialization, \(u\le w\) implies
\[
v(u,t)\ge v(w,t),
\]
because increasing \(u\) relaxes the corresponding constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value or marginal function is obtained by minimizing an extended-real function over the decision variable while retaining the perturbation variable. Its domain records parameters with finite-above value, and its argmin fiber records attainment. For constraint perturbations, infeasibility is represented by positive infinity. Joint convexity passes to the marginal function, while inequality right-hand-side values are coordinatewise nonincreasing under relaxation.
assumptions_latex: The infimum is interpreted in the extended real line.
For the convexity assertion, \(F\) is jointly convex and the marginal function is not identically \(-\infty\).
For monotonicity, the inequality constraints use the convention \(g(x)\le u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p(u)=\inf_xF(x,u),\qquad \operatorname{dom}p=\{u:p(u)<+\infty\},\qquad M(u)=\operatorname*{argmin}_xF(x,u).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(p(u)=\inf\{\alpha:(x,u,\alpha)\in\operatorname{epi}F\text{ for some }x\}\).
When the infimum is attained, \(p(u)=\min_{x\in M(u)}F(x,u)\).
special_cases_latex: Constraint value function: \(p(u)=\inf\{f(x):g(x)\le u\}\).
Partial minimization: \(p(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)\) with no explicit constraints beyond those encoded in \(F\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The nominal optimal value is \(p(0)\).
Convex subgradients of \(p\) provide global affine sensitivity estimates.
boundary_notes: Finite value does not imply that \(M(u)\) is nonempty.
Convexity of \(F\) alone does not guarantee closedness of \(p\).

notation.meaning: The exact minimizing fiber at parameter \(u\).

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph-Projection Closure Equality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projected ordinary epigraph may omit unattained boundary values, but its closure always equals the closure of the marginal epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\), \(U=\mathbb R^m\), let \(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and set \(p(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)\). Assume \(p(u)>-\infty\) for every \(u\). Then \[\operatorname{epi}_{<}p\subseteq\pi_{U\times\mathbb R}(\operatorname{epi}F)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}p,\] and consequently \[\operatorname{cl}\!\left(\pi_{U\times\mathbb R}(\operatorname{epi}F)\right)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{epi}p).\]
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb R^n\), \(U=\mathbb R^m\), and \(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
\(p(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)>-\infty\) for every \(u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}(\pi_{U\times\mathbb R}(\operatorname{epi}F))=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{epi}p).\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: What remains exact when unattained fiber infima remove boundary points from the projected ordinary epigraph.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Minimization Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial minimization projects the effective domain and strict epigraph of the joint function; ordinary epigraph boundary points may be lost when the infimum is unattained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the marginal function by \(p(u)=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u)\). Then its effective domain is the projection \(\operatorname{dom}p=\pi_U(\operatorname{dom}F)\). Moreover, with \(\operatorname{epi}_{<}f=\{(z,r):f(z)<r\}\), partial minimization has the exact geometric representation \[\operatorname{epi}_{<}p=\pi_{U\times\mathbb R}(\operatorname{epi}_{<}F).\] For the ordinary epigraph one always has \(\pi_{U\times\mathbb R}(\operatorname{epi}F)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}p\); equality at a boundary point \((u,p(u))\) requires attainment of the infimum over \(x\).
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(U=\mathbb{R}^m\).
\(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, and \(p(u)=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u)\) never equals \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}p=\pi_U(\operatorname{dom}F)\) and \(\operatorname{epi}_{<}p=\pi_{U\times\mathbb R}(\operatorname{epi}_{<}F)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real partial minimization, including nonattainment of the infimum.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), write its arguments as \((x,z)\), and define \(p(x)=\inf_{z\in\mathbb{R}^m}F(x,z)\). Let \(P(x,z,\alpha)=(x,\alpha)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional epigraph projection for a partial infimum, including the distinction between exact attainment and closure points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The partial-minimization geometry of \(F\) is the projection of its epigraph along the eliminated variable. With
\[
p(x):=\inf_{z\in\mathbb{R}^m}F(x,z),
\qquad
P(x,z,\alpha):=(x,\alpha),
\]
one has
\[
P(\operatorname{epi}F)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}p
\subseteq\operatorname{cl}P(\operatorname{epi}F).
\]
For a fixed \(x\) with \(p(x)\in\mathbb{R}\), the infimum is attained exactly when
\[
(x,p(x))\in P(\operatorname{epi}F).
\]
If the projected epigraph is closed, then
\[
\operatorname{epi}p=P(\operatorname{epi}F),
\]
and every finite marginal value is attained. If \(F\) is convex, then \(p\) is convex because the projection preserves convexity, even though it need not preserve closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial minimization eliminates one block of variables. Geometrically, the epigraph of the resulting marginal function lies between the projection of the original epigraph and the closure of that projection. A finite marginal infimum is attained precisely when its boundary point is actually present in the projected epigraph. Convexity survives projection, whereas closedness and attainment require additional conditions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity and closure of a marginal value function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(p(x)=\inf_zF(x,z)\). Let \(P(x,z,\alpha)=(x,\alpha)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The separate inheritance mechanisms for convexity and lower semicontinuity under finite-dimensional partial minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The value-function convexity-closure coupling is the pair of properties
\[
F\text{ convex}\Longrightarrow p\text{ convex},
\]
and
\[
P(\operatorname{epi}F)\text{ closed}\Longrightarrow
\operatorname{epi}p=P(\operatorname{epi}F)\text{ closed}.
\]
Thus convexity of the marginal follows from convexity of the original epigraph, while lower semicontinuity of the marginal depends on closedness after projection. A sufficient coercive-fiber condition is: \(F\) is closed, proper, and convex, and there exist \(\bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\bar\gamma\in\mathbb{R}\) such that
\[
\{z:F(\bar x,z)\le\bar\gamma\}
\]
is nonempty and compact. Under this condition, \(p\) is closed, proper, and convex, and for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}p\), the set
\[
\operatorname*{argmin}_zF(x,z)
\]
is nonempty and compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity and closedness behave differently under partial minimization. Convexity passes through linear projection directly. Closedness requires the projected epigraph itself to be closed and can fail when minimizing variables escape to infinity. A nonempty compact level set in one eliminated fiber is a standard sufficient condition ensuring that the marginal is closed, proper, and convex and that every finite fiber minimum is attained compactly.
assumptions_latex: For the basic convexity implication, \(F\) is convex.
For the closure-and-attainment conclusion, \(F\) is closed, proper, and convex and has the stated nonempty compact fiber level set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^n),\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_zF(x,z)\neq\varnothing\text{ and is compact for every }x\in\operatorname{dom}p.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Closedness of \(p\) is equivalent to closedness of \(\operatorname{epi}p\).
When \(P(\operatorname{epi}F)\) is closed, \(\operatorname{epi}p=P(\operatorname{epi}F)\).
special_cases_latex: Compactness of all relevant eliminated-variable fibers directly prevents loss of boundary points under projection.
Polyhedral convex epigraphs have closed linear images, so polyhedral marginal functions are closed whenever proper.
immediate_consequences_latex: The compact-fiber condition simultaneously yields lower semicontinuity and attainment.
Without a projection-closedness condition, a closed convex integrand can have a nonclosed marginal.
boundary_notes: The compact-level-set condition is sufficient, not necessary.
The conclusion concerns value-function and fiber-minimizer behavior, not continuity of the full solution mapping.

knowledge_statements.title: Value-Function Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infimum over one block of variables of a jointly convex function is convex in the remaining variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(u_0,u_1\in U\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), the marginal function \(p(u)=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u)\) satisfies \[p((1-\lambda)u_0+\lambda u_1)\leq(1-\lambda)p(u_0)+\lambda p(u_1).\] Thus partial minimization over the full convex space \(X\) preserves convexity. Equivalently, the strict epigraph of \(p\) is a convex projection of the strict epigraph of \(F\). No minimizer of \(F(\cdot,u_i)\) is required to exist.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(U\) are real vector spaces.
\(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex, and \(p(u)=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u)>-\infty\) for every \(u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is convex on \(U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity preservation under partial minimization without an attainment assumption.

knowledge_statements.title: Value-Function Closure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex value function is closed exactly when its epigraph is closed; projecting a closed joint epigraph need not preserve closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The value function \(p\) is closed precisely when it is lower semicontinuous, equivalently when \(\operatorname{epi}p\) is closed in \(U\times\mathbb R\). Although \(F\) is closed, its relevant epigraph projection need not be closed, so closedness is not automatically preserved by partial minimization. When \(p\) is not closed, its lower-semicontinuous hull is characterized by \[\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}p)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{epi}p),\] provided the right-hand side contains no vertical line corresponding to the value \(-\infty\).
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(U=\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(p(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is closed exactly when \(\operatorname{epi}p\) is closed; closedness of \(F\) alone does not ensure this.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness means lower semicontinuity for a proper finite-dimensional convex value function.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity–Closure Interaction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Biconjugation closes a proper convex value function. It leaves the function unchanged exactly when the value function is lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Fenchel biconjugate of \(p\) is its lower-semicontinuous convex hull: \[p^{**}=\operatorname{cl}p.\] Because \(p\) is already convex, closure changes only its lower-semicontinuity defects, and \(p^{**}(u)\leq p(u)\) for every \(u\in\mathbb R^m\). Consequently, \(p=p^{**}\) on all of \(\mathbb R^m\) if and only if \(p\) is closed. At any point where \(p^{**}(u)<p(u)\), convexity persists but epigraphical closure fills a missing boundary value.
assumptions_latex: \(p:\mathbb{R}^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex.
\(p^*(y)=\sup_u\{\langle y,u\rangle-p(u)\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^{**}=\operatorname{cl}p\leq p\), with equality everywhere exactly when \(p\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel–Moreau interaction between convexity and lower-semicontinuous closure.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Value-Function Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex joint indicator can have a nonclosed marginal: projecting the set above produces the open ray of positive parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C=\{(x,u):x>0,\ u\geq 1/x\}\) is closed and convex in \(\mathbb R^2\), hence its indicator \(F=\delta_C\) is proper, closed, and convex. Partial minimization gives \[p(u)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}\delta_C(x,u)=\begin{cases}0,&u>0,\\+\infty,&u\leq0.\end{cases}\] Thus \(p=\delta_{(0,+\infty)}\) is convex but not closed. Its closure is \(\operatorname{cl}p=\delta_{[0,+\infty)}\), showing that closedness can fail solely because projection loses a limiting feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(C=\{(x,u)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ u\geq 1/x\}\).
\(F=\delta_C\) and \(p(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is closed convex, but \(p=\delta_{(0,+\infty)}\) is convex and not closed.

knowledge_statements.title: Marginal-Function Calculus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a marginal is the joint conjugate restricted to zero dual coefficient on the minimized variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(y\in U\), the conjugate of the marginal function satisfies \[p^*(y)=\sup_{u\in U}\{\langle y,u\rangle-p(u)\}=\sup_{(x,u)\in X\times U}\{\langle y,u\rangle-F(x,u)\}=F^*(0,y).\] Hence conjugating an unconstrained partial infimum amounts to restricting the joint conjugate to dual vectors whose component corresponding to \(X\) is zero. In particular, the closed convex hull of the marginal can be recovered as \(p^{**}(u)=\sup_y\{\langle y,u\rangle-F^*(0,y)\}\).
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb R^n\), \(U=\mathbb R^m\), and \(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex.
\(p(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)\) never equals \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*(y)=F^*(0,y)\) for every \(y\in U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugate calculus for an unconstrained finite-dimensional marginal function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential calculus for an attained marginal
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be proper convex, and define \(p(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^m}g(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact subgradient and gradient calculus at parameters where the partial minimum is attained; nonattained and nonconvex marginal rules are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At \(x\in\operatorname{dom}p\), suppose there exists \(\bar y\) with
\[
g(x,\bar y)=p(x).
\]
The marginal-function subdifferential rule is
\[
\partial p(x)=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^n:(s,0)\in\partial g(x,\bar y)\},
\]
under the qualification supporting the exact image-function rule. The zero in the eliminated coordinate expresses stationarity with respect to \(y\). More generally, for \(\varepsilon\ge0\), the corresponding approximate rule is
\[
\partial_{\varepsilon}p(x)=
\{s\in\mathbb{R}^n:(s,0)\in\partial_{\varepsilon}g(x,\bar y)\}
\]
under the stated exactness and relative-interior qualification. If \(g\) is differentiable at \((x,\bar y)\), then \(\nabla_y g(x,\bar y)=0\) and
\[
\nabla p(x)=\nabla_x g(x,\bar y).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a convex marginal infimum is attained, its subgradients are exactly those first-coordinate covectors that extend to a subgradient of the joint function with zero eliminated-coordinate component. The same structure applies to approximate subgradients under the appropriate qualification. In the differentiable case, minimizing over the eliminated variable makes its partial gradient vanish, while the retained partial gradient becomes the gradient of the marginal.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper and convex on the product space.
The marginal infimum is attained at \(\bar y\).
The exact image-function subdifferential qualification holds; one sufficient form is the relevant relative-interior condition on \(\operatorname{dom}g^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial p(x)=\{s:(s,0)\in\partial g(x,\bar y)\},\qquad g(x,\bar y)=p(x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(s\in\partial p(x)\) if and only if \(g(x',y')\ge g(x,\bar y)+\langle s,x'-x\rangle\) for all \((x',y')\).
In the smooth case, \((\nabla p(x),0)=\nabla g(x,\bar y)\).
special_cases_latex: If the minimizing fiber contains several points, the displayed set is independent of the chosen exact minimizer whenever the rule applies.
For differentiable \(g\), every exact minimizer yields the same retained gradient when \(p\) is differentiable.
immediate_consequences_latex: Joint differentiability does not ensure differentiability of the marginal if the infimum is not attained.
The formula converts sensitivity of the marginal into a product-space stationarity condition.
boundary_notes: Attainment is essential for the displayed exact rule.
Additional closure or qualification conditions may be required in infinite-dimensional spaces.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate correspondence between primal and dual values
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), and define \(v(b)=\inf\{f(x):g(x)\le b\}\). Let \(\Phi(\lambda)=\inf_x\{f(x)+\langle\lambda,g(x)\rangle\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inequality-constrained Lagrangian duality expressed through the conjugate and biconjugate of the primal value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The primal-dual value-function correspondence is the conjugate identity
\[
v^*(-\lambda)=
\begin{cases}
-\Phi(\lambda),&\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m,\\
+\infty,&\lambda\notin\mathbb{R}_+^m,
\end{cases}
\]
where
\[
v(b)=\inf\{f(x):g(x)\le b\},
\qquad
\Phi(\lambda)=\inf_x\{f(x)+\langle\lambda,g(x)\rangle\}.
\]
Consequently, the primal value and dual value are
\[
p=v(0),
\qquad
d=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}\Phi(\lambda)=v^{**}(0).
\]
Thus the dual problem evaluates the closed convex envelope of the primal value function at the nominal perturbation. When \(p\in\mathbb{R}\), zero duality gap is the equality
\[
v(0)=v^{**}(0),
\]
which, for a convex value function, is equivalent to lower semicontinuity of \(v\) at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of the right-hand-side value function, evaluated at a negative nonnegative multiplier, is the negative Lagrangian dual function. The nominal primal value is the value function at zero, whereas the dual value is its biconjugate at zero. Hence absence of a duality gap is exactly equality of the value and biconjugate at the nominal parameter; for a finite convex value function this is lower semicontinuity there.
assumptions_latex: The constraint order is componentwise and uses \(g(x)\le b\).
The primal value \(v(0)\) is finite for the lower-semicontinuity equivalence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p=v(0),\qquad d=v^{**}(0),\qquad v^*(-\lambda)=-\Phi(\lambda)\ \text{for }\lambda\ge0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Zero duality gap is \(v(0)=v^{**}(0)\).
When equality holds and a dual optimizer exists, the dual optimal set is \(-\partial v(0)\) after translating the sign convention.
special_cases_latex: If \(v\) is closed proper convex, then \(v=v^{**}\), so the value correspondence has no closure defect.
If \(v\) is not lower semicontinuous at zero, the biconjugate value can be strictly smaller than the primal value.
immediate_consequences_latex: The duality gap is \(v(0)-v^{**}(0)\).
Dual multipliers are supporting covectors of the primal value function with reversed sign.
boundary_notes: The conjugate identity itself does not require convexity of the original data.
Dual attainment and zero gap are distinct properties.

notation.meaning: The Fenchel biconjugate of the primal value function.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Value Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal value function assigns each perturbation the infimum of the perturbed objective, using extended values for infeasibility or unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal value function associated with \(F\) is the extended-real function \[p:U\to[-\infty,+\infty],\qquad p(u)=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u).\] The reference primal problem has value \(p(0_U)\). Its solution set at parameter \(u\) is \(S(u)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}F(x,u)\), which may be empty even when \(p(u)\) is finite. The value \(p(u)=+\infty\) records infeasibility, while \(p(u)=-\infty\) records unboundedness below.

\(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is a proper perturbation function.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Value Attainment Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine lower bounds attaining the dual value are exactly the subgradients of the closed dual value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, let \(d=p^{**}\), and suppose \(d(u)\in\mathbb R\). Then \[\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in\mathbb R^m}\{\langle y,u\rangle-p^*(y)\}=\partial d(u).\] Hence the dual supremum at \(u\) is attained if and only if \(\partial d(u)\neq\varnothing\), and a vector \(y\) attains it exactly when \(d(u)+p^*(y)=\langle y,u\rangle\).
assumptions_latex: \(p:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex.
\(d=p^{**}\) and \(d(u)\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmax}_y\{\langle y,u\rangle-p^*(y)\}=\partial d(u).\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes affine minorants that attain the dual value at a parameter.

notation.meaning: Subdifferential of the dual value function at u

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Value Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual value is the supremum of affine lower bounds generated by the restricted joint conjugate, and it equals the primal value's biconjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual value function induced by the perturbation representation is \[d(u)=\sup_{y\in\mathbb R^m}\{\langle y,u\rangle-F^*(0,y)\}.\] Each feasible \(y\) supplies an affine lower bound \(u'\mapsto\langle y,u'\rangle-F^*(0,y)\) on the primal value function. Since \(p^*(y)=F^*(0,y)\), one has \(d=p^{**}\), and therefore \(d(u)\leq p(u)\) for every \(u\). The supremum may be unattained; the set of maximizing dual vectors is allowed to be empty.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex.
\(p(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(u)=\sup_y\{\langle y,u\rangle-F^*(0,y)\}=p^{**}(u)\leq p(u)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel perturbation dual value at every parameter, not only at the origin.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Value Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual value function equals the closed convex hull of the primal value function, so equality holds precisely where closure does not lower the primal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Marginal conjugacy gives \(p^*(y)=F^*(0,y)\), and hence \[d(u)=\sup_y\{\langle y,u\rangle-F^*(0,y)\}=p^{**}(u)=(\operatorname{cl}p)(u).\] Therefore the dual value function is exactly the closed convex regularization of the primal value function. At a parameter \(u\), primal and dual values coincide if and only if \(p(u)=(\operatorname{cl}p)(u)\). In particular, if \(p\) is closed, then \(p=d\) everywhere; otherwise equality can still hold away from the lower-semicontinuity defects.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex.
\(p(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)\) is proper, and \(d(u)=\sup_y\{\langle y,u\rangle-F^*(0,y)\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(d=p^{**}=\operatorname{cl}p\), a primal-dual value mismatch at \(u\) occurs exactly when \[d(u)=(\operatorname{cl}p)(u)<p(u).\] Thus, for a proper convex perturbational value function, the mismatch boundary is failure of equality with its lower-semicontinuous hull at the parameter under consideration. The mismatch may be finite, or it may have the extended form \(d(u)<+\infty=p(u)\). When \(p(u)=(\operatorname{cl}p)(u)\), this closure-induced mismatch vanishes, independently of whether either primal or dual optimizers are attained.
assumptions_latex: \(p:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(u)<p(u)\) precisely when \((\operatorname{cl}p)(u)<p(u)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mismatch caused by failure of lower semicontinuity in the primal value function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sensitivity subgradient of an optimal-value function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(v:\mathbb{R}^r\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be a proper convex value function and let \(\bar u\in\operatorname{dom}v\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex first-order sensitivity of the optimal value, not generalized derivatives of the solution mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A sensitivity subgradient of \(v\) at \(\bar u\) is a vector \(s\in\mathbb{R}^r\) satisfying
\[
v(u)\ge v(\bar u)+\langle s,u-\bar u\rangle
\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb{R}^r.
\]
The sensitivity-subgradient set is therefore
\[
\partial v(\bar u)=
\{s:v(u)-v(\bar u)\ge\langle s,u-\bar u\rangle\ \forall u\}.
\]
Its elements are global affine lower estimators of the perturbed optimal value. For the constraint value function
\[
v(u,t)=\inf\{f(x):g(x)\le u,\ Ax+b=t\},
\]
and an attained dual solution \((y,z)\) under finite strong duality, the sign convention gives
\[
-(y,z)\in\partial v(0,0).
\]
If \(v\) is differentiable at \(\bar u\), then the sensitivity set is the singleton \(\{\nabla v(\bar u)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sensitivity subgradient is a covector whose affine function supports the optimal-value function from below at the base perturbation. It provides a global first-order lower bound, not merely a local approximation. Under finite strong duality and dual attainment, the negative of an optimal multiplier vector is a sensitivity subgradient at the nominal right-hand side. Differentiability reduces the set to the ordinary gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(v\) is proper and convex.
\(v(\bar u)\in\mathbb{R}\).
For the multiplier specialization, the primal and dual optimal values are finite and equal and the dual optimal set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[s\in\partial v(\bar u)\iff v(u)\ge v(\bar u)+\langle s,u-\bar u\rangle\quad\forall u.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(s\in\partial v(\bar u)\) if and only if \(v(\bar u)+v^*(s)=\langle s,\bar u\rangle\).
At the nominal constraint parameter, \(-(y,z)\in\partial v(0,0)\) is equivalent to \(v(u,t)\ge v(0,0)-y^Tu-z^Tt\).
special_cases_latex: For one scalar perturbation, \(\partial v(\bar u)\) is the interval between the left and right slopes when both are finite.
If \(v\) is differentiable, the unique sensitivity subgradient is its gradient.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every sensitivity subgradient yields a certified lower bound for every perturbed value.
A non-singleton subdifferential represents multiple valid first-order sensitivity covectors.
boundary_notes: A subgradient can exist at a domain boundary without finite sensitivity in every direction.
The definition does not provide an upper error bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier–Subgradient Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an attained minimizer, value-function subgradients are exactly joint subgradients whose component in the minimized variables is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an attained minimizer \(x_u\), a vector \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) is a subgradient of the value function at \(u\) exactly when \[(0,y)\in\partial F(x_u,u).\] Equivalently, \(y\in\partial p(u)\) precisely when \[F(x,u')\geq p(u)+\langle y,u'-u\rangle\qquad\text{for all }(x,u')\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m.\] Hence the perturbation multiplier is a supporting slope of the value function, while its zero component in the \(x\)-coordinates records primal optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex.
\(p(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)\), and \(x_u\in\operatorname*{argmin}_xF(x,u)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\in\partial p(u)\) if and only if \((0,y)\in\partial F(x_u,u)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact multiplier characterization at an attained primal minimizer.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(v(u,t)=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ g(x)\le u,\ Ax+b=t\}\), and let \(D^*\) be the optimal set of the Lagrangian dual with multipliers \((y,z)\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\times\mathbb{R}^p\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact set correspondence under finite strong duality and dual attainment for convex right-hand-side perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The multiplier-subgradient correspondence at the nominal parameter is the set identity
\[
D^*=\{(y,z)\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\times\mathbb{R}^p:-(y,z)\in\partial v(0,0)\}.
\]
Equivalently, \((y,z)\) is dual optimal exactly when
\[
v(u,t)\ge v(0,0)-\langle y,u\rangle-\langle z,t\rangle
\qquad\text{for every }(u,t)\in\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^p.
\]
The negative sign is determined by the convention that positive \(u_i\) relaxs the inequality \(g_i(x)\le u_i\). Consequently,
\[
-D^*=\partial v(0,0)
\]
when every subgradient has a nonpositive inequality component, as follows from the coordinatewise nonincreasing behavior of \(v\) in \(u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the standard right-hand-side perturbation convention, an optimal dual multiplier vector corresponds exactly to the negative of a subgradient of the value function at the nominal parameter. The correspondence is set-valued: multiple dual optimizers give multiple supporting covectors. Its defining inequality is a global lower bound on all perturbed values. The sign reflects that positive inequality perturbations relax constraints.
assumptions_latex: The value function is generated by convex objective and constraint data over a nonempty convex set.
The primal and dual optimal values at \((0,0)\) are finite and equal.
The dual optimal set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(y,z)\in D^*\iff -(y,z)\in\partial v(0,0).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \((y,z)\in D^*\) if and only if \(v(u,t)\ge v(0,0)-y^Tu-z^Tt\) for all \((u,t)\).
If \(v\) is differentiable at zero, then every optimal multiplier equals \(-\nabla v(0,0)\), so the dual optimizer is unique.
special_cases_latex: With no equality constraints, \(D^*=\{y\ge0:-y\in\partial v(0)\}\).
For a single inequality, the optimal multiplier is the negative slope when the value function is differentiable.
immediate_consequences_latex: Dual multipliers certify global sensitivity inequalities.
Nonuniqueness of multipliers is equivalent to nonsingleton value subdifferential under the exact correspondence.
boundary_notes: Strong duality without dual attainment does not yield a multiplier in the subdifferential through this set identity.
Changing the perturbation sign convention reverses the displayed sign.

notation.meaning: The set of optimal Lagrangian multiplier pairs.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Sided Directional Differentiability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex value function is differentiable along a line exactly when all of its shadow prices predict the same rate in that direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, \(u\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}p)\), and \(h\in\mathbb R^m\). Then \(t\mapsto p(u+th)\) is differentiable at \(0\) if and only if \(\langle y,h\rangle\) has the same value for every \(y\in\partial p(u)\). Equivalently, \[\sup_{y\in\partial p(u)}\langle y,h\rangle=\inf_{y\in\partial p(u)}\langle y,h\rangle.\] The common value is the two-sided derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(p:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex.
\(u\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}p)\) and \(h\in\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\mapsto p(u+th)\text{ is differentiable at }0\iff\{\langle y,h\rangle:y\in\partial p(u)\}\text{ is a singleton}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact condition under which one-sided convex value sensitivity extends to differentiation along a line.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Value Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional derivative of a closed convex value function is the support function of its subgradient, or shadow-price, set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every direction \(h\in\mathbb R^m\), the one-sided limit \[p'(u;h)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{p(u+th)-p(u)}{t}\] exists in \(( -\infty,+\infty]\) and is the support function of the value-function subdifferential: \[p'(u;h)=\sigma_{\partial p(u)}(h)=\sup_{y\in\partial p(u)}\langle y,h\rangle.\] Thus each subgradient gives a lower first-order sensitivity, and the largest pairing gives the exact directional rate. When the subdifferential consists of one vector \(y\), the directional rate is \(\langle y,h\rangle\) in every direction.
assumptions_latex: \(p:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(u\in\operatorname{dom}p\) and \(\partial p(u)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p'(u;h)=\sup_{y\in\partial p(u)}\langle y,h\rangle\) for every \(h\in\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided directional sensitivity represented by the shadow-price set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-sided directional sensitivity of a value function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(v:\mathbb{R}^r\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex, let \(\bar u\in\operatorname{dom}v\), and let \(d\in\mathbb{R}^r\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided first-order change of a convex optimal-value function along a fixed perturbation direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The directional value sensitivity of \(v\) at \(\bar u\) in direction \(d\) is the one-sided directional derivative
\[
v'(\bar u;d):=
\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}
\frac{v(\bar u+\alpha d)-v(\bar u)}{\alpha}.
\]
For a proper convex value function this extended-real limit exists and also satisfies
\[
v'(\bar u;d)=
\inf_{\alpha>0}
\frac{v(\bar u+\alpha d)-v(\bar u)}{\alpha}.
\]
If \(\bar u\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}v)\), then the directional derivative is the support function of the sensitivity-subgradient set:
\[
v'(\bar u;d)=
\sup_{s\in\partial v(\bar u)}\langle s,d\rangle.
\]
At other domain points, the closure of \(d\mapsto v'(\bar u;d)\), rather than the raw directional derivative, is generally the support function of \(\partial v(\bar u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional value sensitivity is the limiting change in optimal value per unit positive displacement along a specified perturbation direction. Convexity ensures that this one-sided extended-real limit exists and equals the infimum of the corresponding secant slopes. At relative-interior parameters, it is the support function of the value-function subdifferential. At boundary parameters, the unclosed directional derivative can be strictly larger in inaccessible directions.
assumptions_latex: \(v\) is proper and convex.
\(\bar u\in\operatorname{dom}v\).
For the exact support-function formula, \(\bar u\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}v)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[v'(\bar u;d)=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{v(\bar u+\alpha d)-v(\bar u)}{\alpha}=\sup_{s\in\partial v(\bar u)}\langle s,d\rangle.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For convex \(v\), \(v'(\bar u;d)=\inf_{\alpha>0}[v(\bar u+\alpha d)-v(\bar u)]/\alpha\).
If \(v\) is differentiable at \(\bar u\), then \(v'(\bar u;d)=\langle\nabla v(\bar u),d\rangle\).
special_cases_latex: For a constraint value function with multiplier set \(D^*\), \(v'(0;d)=\sup_{\mu\in D^*}\langle-\mu,d\rangle\) under the exact multiplier-subgradient correspondence and relative-interior hypothesis.
For scalar \(u\), directions \(d=1\) and \(d=-1\) encode the right and negative-left slopes.
immediate_consequences_latex: A finite directional derivative gives the first-order optimal-value change along that direction.
Nondifferentiability permits different multipliers to dominate different directions.
boundary_notes: The derivative can equal \(+\infty\) when the ray immediately leaves the effective domain.
At a domain boundary, the raw derivative need not equal the support function without closure.

notation.meaning: The one-sided directional derivative of the value function.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Shadow-Price Failures
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a boundary point a closed convex value function can have either no shadow price or an unbounded shadow-price set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R\), let \(v_1(t)=-\sqrt t\) for \(t\ge0\) and \(v_1(t)=+\infty\) for \(t<0\). Then \(v_1\) is proper, closed, and convex but \(\partial v_1(0)=\varnothing\). In contrast, for \(v_2=\delta_{[0,+\infty)}\), one has \(\partial v_2(0)=(-\infty,0]\), which is nonempty and unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial v_1(0)=\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad\partial v_2(0)=(-\infty,0].\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that domain membership alone guarantees neither existence nor boundedness of prices.

knowledge_statements.title: Shadow-Price Set Definition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The shadow-price set is the subdifferential of the convex perturbation value function, with its sign determined by the perturbation convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex and let \(\bar u\in\operatorname{dom}v\). Under the convention that the perturbation is the argument \(u\), define \[\mathcal P(\bar u):=\partial v(\bar u)=\{q\in\mathbb R^m:v(u)\ge v(\bar u)+\langle q,u-\bar u\rangle\ \text{for every }u\in\mathbb R^m\}.\] Thus membership is equivalent to a global affine lower sensitivity bound. If the model uses the reversed parameterization \(u=-r\), the corresponding prices with respect to \(r\) are \(-q\).
assumptions_latex: \(v:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex.
\(\bar u\in\operatorname{dom}v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P(\bar u)=\partial v(\bar u)=\{q:v(u)\ge v(\bar u)+\langle q,u-\bar u\rangle\ \forall u\in\mathbb R^m\}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional definition with explicit pairing and perturbation-sign convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Shadow-Price Set Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shadow-price sets are closed and convex; at an interior domain point they are nonempty and compact, while boundary sets may be empty or unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\bar u\in\operatorname{dom}v\), the shadow-price set \(\mathcal P(\bar u)=\partial v(\bar u)\) is closed and convex, although it may be empty or unbounded. If \(\bar u\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}v)\), then \(v\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar u\) and \(\mathcal P(\bar u)\) is nonempty and compact.
assumptions_latex: \(v:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex.
\(\bar u\in\operatorname{dom}v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P(\bar u)\text{ is closed and convex};\quad \bar u\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}v)\Rightarrow \mathcal P(\bar u)\text{ is nonempty and compact}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness, convexity, and the standard interior-point existence and boundedness regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Shadow-Price Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shadow prices defined intrinsically as convex subgradients of the perturbational value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a proper convex value function and let \(\bar u\in\operatorname{dom}p\). The shadow-price set at \(\bar u\) is
\[
S(\bar u):=\partial p(\bar u)
=\{y\in\mathbb R^m:p(u)\ge p(\bar u)+\langle y,u-\bar u\rangle\ \text{for all }u\in\mathbb R^m\}.
\]
Each \(y\in S(\bar u)\) supplies a global affine lower estimate of the change in optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The shadow-price set consists of all vectors giving global affine lower bounds on the convex value function at the reference parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(p:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex.
\(\bar u\in\operatorname{dom}p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(\bar u)=\partial p(\bar u)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stable convex optimization problem via its value function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(v:U\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be a convex perturbation value function on a finite-dimensional space, and let \(\bar u\in U\) satisfy \(v(\bar u)\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical convex-duality stability at a base parameter, defined by existence of a supporting value covector; stronger calmness and Lipschitz notions are separate refinements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The perturbed optimization problem is stable at \(\bar u\) when its value function has a nonempty convex subdifferential there:
\[
\partial v(\bar u)\neq\varnothing.
\]
Equivalently, there exists \(s\in U\) such that
\[
v(u)\ge v(\bar u)+\langle s,u-\bar u\rangle
\qquad\text{for every }u\in U.
\]
The set of all such stability covectors is \(\partial v(\bar u)\). At the nominal parameter \(\bar u=0\), and under the Lagrangian sign convention for relaxed right-hand sides, stability is equivalent to existence of a dual optimal multiplier when finite strong duality holds:
\[
D^*=-\partial v(0).
\]
This definition supplies a finite affine lower support to the optimal value. It does not, by itself, require a two-sided Lipschitz estimate or continuity of minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the classical convex-duality sense, an optimization problem is stable at a perturbation parameter when the value function has at least one subgradient there. This means that the value admits a global affine lower support at the base parameter. Under finite strong duality, the stability covectors correspond with reversed sign to attained optimal multipliers. Stability in this sense is weaker than local Lipschitz continuity and concerns values rather than solution mappings.
assumptions_latex: \(v\) is convex and \(v(\bar u)\) is finite.
For the multiplier equivalence, finite strong duality holds and the standard right-hand-side sign convention is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{stable at }\bar u\iff\partial v(\bar u)\neq\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Stability is equivalent to the existence of a continuous affine minorant touching \(v\) at \(\bar u\).
Under finite zero duality gap, stability at zero is equivalent to dual attainment.
special_cases_latex: If \(\bar u\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}v)\), a proper convex value function has a nonempty subdifferential there.
Differentiability at \(\bar u\) implies stability with the unique covector \(\nabla v(\bar u)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every stability covector supplies a global lower sensitivity bound.
Stable finite convex programs possess a first-order dual certificate at the base parameter.
boundary_notes: This classical definition is not synonymous with Lipschitz stability, calmness, or semicontinuity.
A stable problem can still have a discontinuous or set-valued optimizer mapping.

notation.meaning: The dual optimal multiplier set at the nominal parameter.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Objective with a Non-Lower-Semicontinuous Value
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint continuity does not ensure lower semicontinuity of the value when nearby optimizers escape to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x,u)=(ux-1)^2\) on \(\mathbb R^2\), \(F\) is continuous, but \(v(u):=\inf_xF(x,u)\) equals \(0\) for \(u\neq0\) and \(1\) for \(u=0\). Hence \(v\) is not lower semicontinuous at \(0\), while the optimizers \(x=1/u\) escape as \(u\to0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Escape-to-infinity failure of marginal lower semicontinuity.

knowledge_statements.title: Semicontinuity Tests for Optimal Values
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower semicontinuity prevents downward jumps, upper semicontinuity prevents upward jumps, and together they give continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A value function \(v\) is lower semicontinuous at \(\bar u\) exactly when \(v(\bar u)\leq\liminf_n v(u_n)\) for every \(u_n\to\bar u\), and upper semicontinuous there exactly when \(v(\bar u)\geq\limsup_n v(u_n)\). It is continuous at \(\bar u\) exactly when both conditions hold and \(v(\bar u)\) is finite.
assumptions_latex: The parameter space is finite-dimensional or, more generally, metrizable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lsc}_{\bar u}v\iff v(\bar u)\leq\liminf_n v(u_n)\), and \(\operatorname{usc}_{\bar u}v\iff v(\bar u)\geq\limsup_n v(u_n)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential lower- and upper-semicontinuity criteria in finite-dimensional parameter spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Upper Semicontinuity from a Nominal Competitor
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nominal optimizer that remains an upper-semicontinuous competitor prevents nearby optimal values from jumping upward.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)\), and suppose \(F(\bar x,\bar u)=v(\bar u)\). If \(u\mapsto F(\bar x,u)\) is upper semicontinuous at \(\bar u\), then \(\limsup_{u\to\bar u}v(u)\leq v(\bar u)\).
assumptions_latex: \(v(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)\).
\(F(\bar x,\bar u)=v(\bar u)\).
\(u\mapsto F(\bar x,u)\) is upper semicontinuous at \(\bar u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle\limsup_{u\to\bar u}v(u)\leq v(\bar u)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper-semicontinuity criterion using an attained nominal optimizer.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower Semicontinuity from Uniform Level Boundedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A jointly lower-semicontinuous objective has a lower-semicontinuous value when nearby bounded-value solutions cannot escape.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous and \(v(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)\). If, for every real \(\alpha\), the sets \(\{x:F(x,u)\leq\alpha\}\) are uniformly bounded for \(u\) near \(\bar u\), and \(v\) is proper near \(\bar u\), then \(v\) is lower semicontinuous at \(\bar u\).
assumptions_latex: \(X,U\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces and \(F\) is lower semicontinuous.
Nearby sublevel sets are locally uniformly bounded at every finite level.
\(v(u):=\inf_xF(x,u)\) is proper near \(\bar u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(\bar u)\leq\liminf_{u\to\bar u}v(u)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional inf-projection theorem preventing bounded-value near-minimizers from escaping.

knowledge_statements.title: Semicontinuity of Optimal Values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sequential compactness criterion for lower semicontinuity of infimal value functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(U\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous, and define \(p(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)\). Fix \(\bar u\) with \(p(\bar u)\in\mathbb R\). Suppose that whenever \(u_k\to\bar u\) and \(F(x_k,u_k)\) is bounded above, the sequence \((x_k)\) has a convergent subsequence. Then
\[
p(\bar u)\le\liminf_{k\to\infty}p(u_k)
\]
for every sequence \(u_k\to\bar u\); hence \(p\) is lower semicontinuous at \(\bar u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower semicontinuity of the objective plus local compactness of approximate minimizers implies lower semicontinuity of the optimal-value function.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is lower semicontinuous.
\(p(\bar u)\in\mathbb R\).
Bounded-level sequences over parameters converging to \(\bar u\) are relatively compact in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(\bar u)\le\liminf_k p(u_k)\) whenever \(u_k\to\bar u\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Joint Continuity Does Not Ensure Lower Semicontinuity of the Value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Escape-to-infinity counterexample for marginal lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x,u):=(ux-1)^2\) on \(\mathbb R^2\), the function \(F\) is continuous, but its marginal value satisfies \[v(u):=\inf_xF(x,u)=\begin{cases}0,&u\neq0,\\1,&u=0.\end{cases}\] Thus \(v\) is not lower semicontinuous at \(0\); for \(u\neq0\), its optimizer \(x=1/u\) escapes to infinity as \(u\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A jointly continuous objective can have a non-lower-semicontinuous optimal value when nearby optimizers escape to infinity.
knowledge_statements.title: Joint Continuity Does Not Ensure Lower Semicontinuity of the Value

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper Semicontinuity from a Stable Nominal Competitor
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A complementary upper-semicontinuity criterion for a marginal optimal-value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v(u):=\inf_xF(x,u)\), and suppose \(\bar x\) attains \(v(\bar u)\). If \(u\mapsto F(\bar x,u)\) is upper semicontinuous at \(\bar u\), then \[\limsup_{u\to\bar u}v(u)\leq v(\bar u).\] Combined with lower semicontinuity of \(v\), this yields continuity at \(\bar u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nominal optimizer that remains an upper-semicontinuous competitor prevents nearby optimal values from jumping upward.
assumptions_latex: \(v(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)\).
\(F(\bar x,\bar u)=v(\bar u)\).
The mapping \(u\mapsto F(\bar x,u)\) is upper semicontinuous at \(\bar u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle\limsup_{u\to\bar u}v(u)\leq v(\bar u)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Upper Semicontinuity from a Stable Nominal Competitor
Calmness without Neighborhood Lipschitz Continuity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic deviation from the reference point can coexist with oscillations too rapid for pairwise Lipschitz control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(v(0)=0\) and \(v(u)=u^2\sin(1/u^2)\) for \(u\neq0\). Then \(v\) is calm at \(0\), but it is not Lipschitz on any neighborhood of \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is calm at \(0\) but not locally Lipschitz around \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict separation of fixed-base calmness from pairwise local Lipschitz stability.

knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Calmness and Calmness Modulus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Calmness gives a linear value bound relative to one fixed parameter; its modulus is the least local bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A value function \(v\) is calm at \(\bar u\) if it is finite on a neighborhood of \(\bar u\) and there exist \(\kappa\geq0\) and \(r>0\) such that \(|v(u)-v(\bar u)|\leq\kappa\|u-\bar u\|\) whenever \(\|u-\bar u\|<r\). The infimum of admissible \(\kappa\) is \(\operatorname{clm}v(\bar u)\).
assumptions_latex: \(v\) is real-valued near \(\bar u\) in a normed parameter space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{clm}v(\bar u):=\inf\{\kappa:\ |v(u)-v(\bar u)|\leq\kappa\|u-\bar u\|\text{ locally}\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided fixed-base calmness for a finite scalar value function.

knowledge_statements.title: Calmness of Value Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided local linear stability at a reference perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A proper value function \(p:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is calm from below at \(\bar u\in\operatorname{dom}p\) if there exist \(L\ge0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that
\[
p(u)\ge p(\bar u)-L\lVert u-\bar u\rVert
\]
for every \(u\in\operatorname{dom}p\) with \(\lVert u-\bar u\rVert<\varepsilon\). Equivalently,
\[
\liminf_{\substack{u\to\bar u\\u\ne\bar u}}
\frac{p(u)-p(\bar u)}{\lVert u-\bar u\rVert}>-\infty.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Calmness from below means the optimal value cannot decrease faster than linearly under sufficiently small perturbations.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is proper.
\(\bar u\in\operatorname{dom}p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(u)\ge p(\bar u)-L\lVert u-\bar u\rVert\) locally for some \(L\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Calmness Does Not Imply Neighborhood Lipschitz Continuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonconvex scalar example separating fixed-base calmness from pairwise local Lipschitz stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(v(0)=0\) and \(v(u)=u^2\sin(1/u^2)\) for \(u\neq0\). Then \(v\) is calm at \(0\), since \(|v(u)-v(0)|\leq |u|^2\), but \(v\) is not Lipschitz on any neighborhood of \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function can vary only quadratically from one reference point while still oscillating too rapidly to be Lipschitz between nearby points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is calm at \(0\) but is not locally Lipschitz around \(0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Calmness Does Not Imply Neighborhood Lipschitz Continuity
Local Lipschitz Value Stability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local Lipschitz stability uniformly controls the value difference between every pair of nearby parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A value function \(v\) is locally Lipschitz around \(\bar u\) if there exist \(L\geq0\) and \(r>0\) such that \(|v(u)-v(w)|\leq L\|u-w\|\) for all \(u,w\in B_r(\bar u)\). This implies continuity and calmness at every point of a smaller neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: \(v\) is real-valued on a neighborhood of \(\bar u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists L,r>0\ \forall u,w\in B_r(\bar u): |v(u)-v(w)|\leq L\|u-w\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise local Lipschitz regularity of a finite value function.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Subgradient Lipschitz Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex value function is Lipschitz exactly when its supporting slopes are uniformly bounded, and it is locally Lipschitz in its relative-domain interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(O\) be open and convex in a finite-dimensional normed space and let \(v:O\to\mathbb R\) be convex. Then \(v\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(O\) if and only if \(\|y\|_*\leq L\) for every \(u\in O\) and \(y\in\partial v(u)\). Consequently, every proper convex function is locally Lipschitz on \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}v)\), relative to its affine hull.
assumptions_latex: \(O\) is open and convex in a finite-dimensional normed space.
\(v:O\to\mathbb R\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\text{ is }L\text{-Lipschitz on }O\iff\sup\{\|y\|_*:u\in O,\ y\in\partial v(u)\}\leq L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex subgradient characterization on an open convex region.

knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Value Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local Lipschitz stability characterized by uniformly bounded convex subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) be convex on an open convex neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar u\). For an open neighborhood \(W\) with closure contained in \(V\), if
\[
M:=\sup\{\lVert y\rVert:u\in W,\ y\in\partial p(u)\}<+\infty,
\]
then
\[
|p(u)-p(v)|\le M\lVert u-v\rVert
\]
for all \(u,v\in W\) whose connecting segment lies in \(W\). Conversely, local \(L\)-Lipschitz continuity implies \(\lVert y\rVert\le L\) for every subgradient at interior points of that neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex value function is locally Lipschitz precisely when its nearby subgradients are uniformly bounded; their norms control the Lipschitz modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is finite and convex on an open convex neighborhood \(V\).
\(\overline W\subset V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform boundedness of \(\partial p(u)\) on \(W\) yields local Lipschitz stability, with the converse bound at interior points.

notation.meaning: uniform bound on nearby subgradient norms

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Subgradient Criterion for Lipschitz Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgradient characterization of pairwise Lipschitz continuity for a finite convex value function on an open convex region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(O\) be an open convex subset of a finite-dimensional normed space and let \(v:O\to\mathbb R\) be convex. For \(L\geq0\), \(v\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(O\) if and only if \[\|y\|_*\leq L\quad\text{for every }u\in O\text{ and }y\in\partial v(u).\] Consequently, every proper convex value function is locally Lipschitz on \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}v)\), relative to its affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex value function is Lipschitz exactly when all of its local supporting slopes are uniformly bounded; convex functions are therefore locally Lipschitz inside their relative domains.
assumptions_latex: \(O\) is open and convex in a finite-dimensional normed space.
\(v:O\to\mathbb R\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\text{ is }L\text{-Lipschitz on }O\iff\sup\{\|y\|_*:u\in O,\ y\in\partial v(u)\}\leq L\).

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of the value function

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Subgradient Criterion for Lipschitz Stability
Relative Continuity without Linear Boundary Stability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex value function may be continuous along its domain boundary while its linear sensitivity becomes unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(v(u)=-\sqrt{u}\) for \(u\geq0\) and \(v(u)=+\infty\) for \(u<0\). Then \(v\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and its restriction to \([0,+\infty)\) is continuous at \(0\). Nevertheless, \(|v(u)-v(0)|/|u|=1/\sqrt{u}\to+\infty\) as \(u\downarrow0\), so \(v\) is neither relatively calm nor relatively locally Lipschitz at \(0\).
assumptions_latex: \(v(u)=-\sqrt u\) for \(u\geq0\) and \(v(u)=+\infty\) for \(u<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is relatively continuous at \(0\) but neither relatively calm nor relatively locally Lipschitz there.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex boundary example separating relative continuity from relative calmness and Lipschitz stability.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient Calmness Requires Interior Finiteness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite value cannot be ambiently calm at a domain boundary because arbitrarily close infeasible parameters have infinite value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v:U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) with \(v(\bar u)\in\mathbb R\). If calmness at \(\bar u\) is required with respect to every nearby point of the ambient space, then calmness implies \(\bar u\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}v)\). At a boundary point only a relative-to-domain regularity notion can be possible.
assumptions_latex: \(v:U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(v(\bar u)\in\mathbb R\).
Calmness is measured over every sufficiently near ambient parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\text{ calm at }\bar u\implies\bar u\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}v)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real obstruction to ambient calmness at a finite domain-boundary point.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation-Domain Boundary Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A convex boundary example separating continuity from calmness and Lipschitz stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(p:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by
\[
p(u)=
\begin{cases}
-\sqrt{u},&u\ge0,\\
+\infty,&u<0.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(p\) is proper, closed, and convex, and it is continuous relative to its domain at the boundary point \(0\). Nevertheless,
\[
\frac{|p(u)-p(0)|}{|u|}=\frac1{\sqrt{u}}\to+\infty
\quad\text{as }u\downarrow0.
\]
Consequently \(p\) is neither locally Lipschitz relative to its domain nor calm from below at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a perturbation-domain boundary, a closed convex value function may remain continuous while losing every finite calmness or Lipschitz modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(p(u)=-\sqrt u\) for \(u\ge0\) and \(p(u)=+\infty\) for \(u<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is continuous at \(0\) relative to its domain but is neither calm from below nor locally Lipschitz there.
